# lexopt - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/lexopt/

## Expand description

A pathologically simple command line argument parser.

Most argument parsers are declarative: you tell them what to parse, and they do it.

This one provides you with a stream of options and values and lets you figure out the rest.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
struct Args {
    thing: String,
    number: u32,
    shout: bool,
}
fn parse_args() -> Result<Args, lexopt::Error> {
    use lexopt::prelude::*;
    let mut thing = None;
    let mut number = 1;
    let mut shout = false;
    let mut parser = lexopt::Parser::from_env();
    while let Some(arg) = parser.next()? {
        match arg {
            Short('n') | Long("number") => {
                number = parser.value()?.parse()?;
            }
            Long("shout") => {
                shout = true;
            }
            Value(val) if thing.is_none() => {
                thing = Some(val.string()?);
            }
            Long("help") => {
                println!("Usage: hello [-n|--number=NUM] [--shout] THING");
                std::process::exit(0);
            }
            _ => return Err(arg.unexpected()),
        }
    }
    Ok(Args {
        thing: thing.ok_or("missing argument THING")?,
        number,
        shout,
    })
}
fn main() -> Result<(), lexopt::Error> {
    let args = parse_args()?;
    let mut message = format!("Hello {}", args.thing);
    if args.shout {
        message = message.to_uppercase();
    }
    for _ in 0..args.number {
        println!("{}", message);
    }
    Ok(())
}
```
Let’s walk through this:

- We start parsing with `Parser::from_env`
- We call `parser.next()`
- We match on arguments. `Short``Long`
- To get the value that belongs to an option (like `10`in`-n 10`) we call`parser.value()`- This returns a standard `OsString`
- For convenience, `use lexopt::prelude::*``.parse()``str::parse`
- Calling `parser.value()`is how we tell`Parser`that`-n`takes a value at all.

- This returns a standard
- `Value`indicates a free-standing argument.- `if thing.is_none()`is a useful pattern for positional arguments. If we already found- `thing`we pass it on to another case.
- It also contains an `OsString`.- The `.string()``String`.

- The

- If we don’t know what to do with an argument we use `return Err(arg.unexpected())`
- Strings can be promoted to errors for custom error messages.

# lexopt 0.3.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/lexopt/latest

# Lexopt

Lexopt is an argument parser for Rust. It tries to have the simplest possible design that's still correct. It's so simple that it's a bit tedious to use.

Lexopt is:

- Small: one file, no dependencies, no macros. Easy to audit or vendor.
- Correct: standard conventions are supported and ambiguity is avoided. Tested and fuzzed.
- Pedantic: arguments are returned as `OsString`
- Imperative: options are returned as they are found, nothing is declared ahead of time.
- Minimalist: only basic functionality is provided.
- Unhelpful: there is no help generation and error messages often lack context.

## Example

```
```
Let's walk through this:

- We start parsing with `Parser::from_env()`.
- We call `parser.next()`in a loop to get all the arguments until they run out.
- We match on arguments. `Short`and`Long`indicate an option.
- To get the value that belongs to an option (like `10`in`-n 10`) we call`parser.value()`.- This returns a standard `OsString`- For convenience, `use lexopt::prelude::*`adds a`.parse()`method, analogous to[the one on](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.str.html#method.parse).`&str`

- For convenience,
- Calling `parser.value()`is how we tell`Parser`that`-n`takes a value at all.

- This returns a standard
- `Value`indicates a free-standing argument.- `if thing.is_none()`is a useful pattern for positional arguments. If we already found- `thing`we pass it on to another case.
- It also contains an `OsString`.- The `.string()`method decodes it into a plain`String`.

- The

- If we don't know what to do with an argument we use `return Err(arg.unexpected())`to turn it into an error message.
- Strings can be promoted to errors for custom error messages.

This covers most of the functionality in the library. Lexopt does very little for you.

For a larger example with useful patterns, see [ examples/cargo.rs](https://docs.rs/examples/cargo.rs).

## Command line syntax

The following conventions are supported:

- Short options (`-q`)
- Long options (`--verbose`)
- `--`to mark the end of options
- `=`to separate options from values (- `--option=value`,- `-o=value`)- The nonstandard `-o=value`syntax can be[disabled](https://docs.rs/lexopt/latest/lexopt/struct.Parser.html#method.set_short_equals).

- The nonstandard
- Spaces to separate options from values (`--option value`,`-o value`)
- Unseparated short options (`-ovalue`)
- Combined short options (`-abc`to mean`-a -b -c`)
- Options with optional arguments (like GNU sed's `-i`, which can be used standalone or as`-iSUFFIX`) (`Parser::optional_value()`
- Options with multiple arguments (`Parser::values()`

These are not supported out of the box:

- Single-dash long options (like find's `-name`)
- Abbreviated long options (GNU's getopt lets you write `--num`instead of`--number`if it can be expanded unambiguously)

[ Parser::raw_args()](https://docs.rs/lexopt/latest/lexopt/struct.Parser.html#method.raw_args) and

[provide an escape hatch for consuming the original command line. This can be used for custom syntax, like treating](https://docs.rs/lexopt/latest/lexopt/struct.Parser.html#method.try_raw_args)

`Parser::try_raw_args()``-123` as a number instead of a string of options. See [for an example of this.](https://docs.rs/examples/nonstandard.rs)

`examples/nonstandard.rs`## Unicode

This library supports unicode while tolerating non-unicode arguments.

Short options may be unicode, but only a single codepoint (a `char`).

Options can be combined with non-unicode arguments. That is, `--option=���` will not cause an error or mangle the value.

Options themselves are patched as by [ String::from_utf8_lossy](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/string/struct.String.html#method.from_utf8_lossy) if they're not valid unicode. That typically means you'll raise an error later when they're not recognized.

## Why?

For a particular application I was looking for a small parser that's pedantically correct. There are other compact argument parsing libraries, but I couldn't find one that handled `OsString`s and implemented all the fiddly details of the argument syntax faithfully.

This library may also be useful if a lot of control is desired, like when the exact argument order matters or not all options are known ahead of time. It could be considered more of a lexer than a parser.

## Why not?

This library may not be worth using if:

- You don't care about non-unicode arguments
- You don't care about exact compliance and correctness
- You don't care about code size
- You do care about great error messages
- You hate boilerplate

## See also

- [Collected benchmarks of argument parsing crates](https://github.com/rosetta-rs/argparse-rosetta-rs).
- libc's `getopt`
- Plan 9's *arg(3)*macros

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (c397dae80 2026-07-02)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```

`if var.is_ok `

                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.

                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.

                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|

# cumulus_client_pov_recovery - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cumulus-client-pov-recovery/0.32.0/cumulus_client_pov_recovery/

## Expand description

Parachain PoV recovery

A parachain needs to build PoVs that are send to the relay chain to progress. These PoVs are erasure encoded and one piece of it is stored by each relay chain validator. As the relay chain decides on which PoV per parachain to include and thus, to progress the parachain it can happen that the block corresponding to this PoV isn’t propagated in the parachain network. This can have several reasons, either a malicious collator that managed to include its own PoV and doesn’t want to share it with the rest of the network or maybe a collator went down before it could distribute the block in the network. When something like this happens we can use the PoV recovery algorithm implemented in this crate to recover a PoV and to propagate it with the rest of the network.

It works in the following way:

-
For every included relay chain block we note the backed candidate of our parachain. If the block belonging to the PoV is already known, we do nothing. Otherwise we start a timer that waits for a randomized time inside a specified interval before starting to recover the PoV.
-
If between starting and firing the timer the block is imported, we skip the recovery of the PoV.
-
If the timer fired we recover the PoV using the relay chain PoV recovery protocol.

4a. After it is recovered, we restore the block and import it.

4b. Since we are trying to recover pending candidates, availability is not guaranteed. If the block PoV is not yet available, we retry.

If we need to recover multiple PoV blocks (which should hopefully not happen in real life), we make sure that the blocks are imported in the correct order.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [PoVRecovery](https://docs.rs/struct.PoVRecovery.html)
- Encapsulates the logic of the pov recovery.
- [Recovery](https://docs.rs/struct.RecoveryDelayRange.html)- Delay - Range
- The delay between observing an unknown block and triggering the recovery of a block. Randomizing the start of the recovery within this interval can be used to prevent self-DOSing if the recovery request is part of a distributed protocol and there is the possibility that multiple actors are requiring to perform the recovery action at approximately the same time.
- [Recovery](https://docs.rs/struct.RecoveryRequest.html)- Request
- Structure used to trigger an explicit recovery request via `PoVRecovery`.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Recovery](https://docs.rs/enum.RecoveryKind.html)- Kind
- Type of recovery to trigger.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Recovery](https://docs.rs/trait.RecoveryHandle.html)- Handle
- Test-friendly wrapper trait for the overseer handle. Can be used to simulate failing recovery requests.

# snowbridge_pallet_inbound_queue_v2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/snowbridge-pallet-inbound-queue-v2/0.14.0/snowbridge_pallet_inbound_queue_v2/

## Expand description

Inbound Queue

[§](https://docs.rs#overview)Overview

Receives messages emitted by the Gateway contract on Ethereum, whereupon they are verified, translated to XCM, and finally sent to AssetHub for further processing.

Message relayers are rewarded in wrapped Ether that is included within the message. This wrapped Ether is derived from Ether that the message origin has locked up on Ethereum.

# aegis-id 0.1.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/aegis-id/0.1.0

# Aegis ID

Aegis ID is a terminal password-rule puzzle disguised as a very ordinary account enrollment console.

The program asks for a username and password, then quietly adds increasingly restrictive password requirements. Failed attempts only show the requirements that are currently not satisfied. Once every rule is satisfied, the console clears and asks you to rewrite the password exactly.

# graphtrail - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/graphtrail/0.2.0/graphtrail/

## Expand description

GraphTrail: a local code-graph sidecar. Library crate exposing the extraction, storage, and query layers so the CLI binary, tests, and (later) the MCP server share one API.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [adapters](https://docs.rs/adapters/index.html)
- Optional, feature-gated integrations with external systems. The default build compiles none of these, keeping the core sidecar free of network and cross-tool dependencies.
- [cli](https://docs.rs/cli/index.html)
- Command-line surface and output formatting.
- [extractors](https://docs.rs/extractors/index.html)
- File indexing: language detection and per-file extraction dispatch.
- [mcp](https://docs.rs/mcp/index.html)
- Minimal MCP server: newline-delimited JSON-RPC 2.0 over stdin/stdout, exposing GraphTrail’s read-only queries as tools. No async runtime and no extra dependencies, keeping the sidecar small.
- [model](https://docs.rs/model/index.html)
- Shared plain-data types used across extractors, store, and query layers.
- [query](https://docs.rs/query/index.html)
- Read-only query layer over the graph database.
- [store](https://docs.rs/store/index.html)
- Storage layer: schema, connection lifecycle, and the sync write path.

# oxvif - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/oxvif/0.11.0/oxvif/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#oxvif)oxvif

An async Rust client library for the [ONVIF](https://www.onvif.org) IP camera protocol.

ONVIF (Open Network Video Interface Forum) is the industry standard for interoperability between IP-based security cameras. This library provides a complete async client covering device management, media streaming, PTZ control, imaging, on-screen display, events, recording, search, and replay — all over SOAP/HTTP(S) with WS-Security and HTTP Digest authentication.

[§](https://docs.rs#onvif-profile-coverage)ONVIF Profile coverage

| Profile | Description | Coverage | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Profile S | Video streaming | ~95% | All core operations implemented |
| Profile T | Advanced streaming (H.265, focus, OSD, audio) | ~95% | HTTP Digest Auth, Media2 audio/metadata/analytics config, PTZ compat; Analytics rules and DeviceIO not yet implemented |
| Profile G | Recording & playback | ~85% | Read/search/replay + full recording/job write management; live-source job binding not yet implemented |

[§](https://docs.rs#supported-services)Supported services

- **Device**— capabilities, scopes, device info, hostname, NTP, reboot, user management, network interfaces/protocols/DNS/gateway, relay outputs, storage configurations, system log/URIs, factory default, discovery mode, firmware upgrade / system restore (upload-URI flow), auxiliary commands (wiper/IR lamp)
- **Media1 / Media2**— profiles, RTSP/snapshot URIs, video + audio config, OSD, metadata config, audio decoder/output config, video source modes, unified AddConfiguration/RemoveConfiguration
- **PTZ**— absolute/relative/continuous move, presets, home position, status, configurations, nodes, compatible configurations
- **Imaging**— brightness/contrast/exposure settings, focus move/stop/status
- **Events**— pull-point subscriptions, event polling, renew, unsubscribe, continuous- `event_stream`, synchronization point
- **Recording**— list stored recordings; create/delete recordings, tracks, and recording jobs
- **Search**— find recordings by scope, collect results, end search
- **Replay**— get RTSP playback URI for a stored recording
- **WS-Discovery**— UDP multicast probe to find cameras on the local network

[§](https://docs.rs#optional-features)Optional features

- `health`- `health::HealthCheck`, a fast read-only conformance check that returns a- `health::HealthReport`(per-check Pass/Warn/Fail/Skip plus a Profile S/T/G assessment). Pure library code over- `OnvifSession`- `to_json`/- `to_json_pretty`) and a later report can diff against an earlier one via- `HealthReport::diff`- `examples/healthcheck.rs --baseline <file.json>`.
- `mock`- `mock-server`- `mock`module). The- `mock`feature also exposes- `fixtures::CapturingTransport`/- `fixtures::FixtureTransport`for recording real-camera exchanges into- `tests/fixtures/<vendor>-<model>/`and replaying them in tests without the device (see- `examples/record_fixtures.rs`).

[§](https://docs.rs#architecture)Architecture

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                  OnvifSession                        │
│     caches service URLs — delegates every call       │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                   OnvifClient                        │
│     stateless — you supply service URLs per call     │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│    soap::SoapEnvelope  │  soap::WsSecurityToken      │  ← SOAP layer
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                  Transport trait                     │  ← HTTP abstraction
│          (HttpTransport / mock in tests)             │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick start

Two ways to use oxvif — pick whichever suits your workflow.

[§](https://docs.rs#onvifsession--url-caching-handled-for-you)`OnvifSession` — URL caching handled for you

[ OnvifSession](https://docs.rs/session/struct.OnvifSession.html) calls

`GetCapabilities` once at construction and caches all
service URLs. No URL parameters needed for individual methods.```
use oxvif::{OnvifSession, OnvifError};
async fn run() -> Result<(), OnvifError> {
    let session = OnvifSession::builder("http://192.168.1.100/onvif/device_service")
        .with_credentials("admin", "password")
        .with_clock_sync()  // syncs WS-Security timestamp with device clock
        .build()
        .await?;
    let profiles = session.get_profiles().await?;
    let uri = session.get_stream_uri(&profiles[0].token).await?;
    println!("RTSP stream: {}", uri.uri);
    let status = session.ptz_get_status(&profiles[0].token).await?;
    println!("Pan: {:?}  Tilt: {:?}", status.pan, status.tilt);
    Ok(())
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#onvifclient--direct-control-you-manage-service-urls)`OnvifClient` — direct control, you manage service URLs

[ OnvifClient](https://docs.rs/client/struct.OnvifClient.html) is stateless and gives direct control over every call.
You fetch and forward service URLs yourself for full routing control.

```
use oxvif::{OnvifClient, OnvifError};
async fn run() -> Result<(), OnvifError> {
    let client = OnvifClient::new("http://192.168.1.100/onvif/device_service")
        .with_credentials("admin", "password");
    let dt = client.get_system_date_and_time().await?;
    let client = client.with_utc_offset(dt.utc_offset_secs());
    let caps = client.get_capabilities().await?;
    let media_url = caps.media.url.as_deref().unwrap();
    let profiles = client.get_profiles(media_url).await?;
    let uri = client.get_stream_uri(media_url, &profiles[0].token).await?;
    println!("RTSP stream: {}", uri.uri);
    Ok(())
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#testing-without-a-real-camera)Testing without a real camera

Enable the ** mock** feature for a built-in, stateful mock ONVIF device and
drive an

[against it — no network, no real camera. The](https://docs.rs/client/struct.OnvifClient.html)

`OnvifClient`**feature additionally provides a bound-port**

`mock-server``mock::MockServer`
for cross-process / non-Rust clients. See the `mock` module for details.[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// Cargo.toml:  oxvif = { version = "0.9", features = ["mock"] }
use std::sync::Arc;
use oxvif::{OnvifClient, mock::MockTransport};
let client = OnvifClient::new("http://mock")
    .with_transport(Arc::new(MockTransport::new()));
// exercise client commands — Set persists, Get reflects it.
```
For full control you can instead implement [ transport::Transport](https://docs.rs/transport/trait.Transport.html) yourself
to inject any fixture:

```
use oxvif::transport::{Transport, TransportError};
use async_trait::async_trait;
use std::sync::Arc;
struct FixtureTransport { xml: String }
#[async_trait]
impl Transport for FixtureTransport {
    async fn soap_post(&self, _url: &str, _action: &str, _body: String)
        -> Result<String, TransportError>
    {
        Ok(self.xml.clone())
    }
}
let client = oxvif::OnvifClient::new("http://ignored")
    .with_transport(Arc::new(FixtureTransport { xml: "<s:Envelope/>".into() }));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#health--conformance-checks)Health & conformance checks

Enable the ** health** feature for

[— a fast, read-only conformance check that reports Pass/Warn/Fail/Skip per ONVIF service plus a Profile S/T/G verdict. It includes a](https://docs.rs/health/struct.HealthCheck.html)

`health::HealthCheck`**parse-coverage**dimension that flags when a parser silently drops list data (a wrong element name returning an empty result with no error). To validate the parsers against real hardware, the

`conformance` example dumps each device’s raw
responses next to the parsed summary so silent-parse gaps stand out.## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

# rsclaw-migrate 0.1.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rsclaw-migrate/0.1.0

Please check the

[build logs](https://docs.rs/crate/rsclaw-migrate/0.1.0/builds)for more information.

See

[Builds](https://docs.rs/about/builds)for ideas on how to fix a failed build, or

[Metadata](https://docs.rs/about/metadata)for how to configure docs.rs builds.

If you believe this is docs.rs' fault,

[open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose).

OpenClaw data migration module.

Provides three migration modes for transitioning from OpenClaw to rsclaw:

- `Seamless`: coexist with OpenClaw, sharing base directory
- `Import`: copy all OpenClaw data into rsclaw's own stores
- `New`: ignore OpenClaw data entirely, start new

OpenClaw stores data as JSONL files, not SQLite. The directory layout is: ~/.openclaw/ openclaw.json # Main config agents/<agent_id>/sessions/sessions.json # Session index agents/<agent_id>/sessions/.jsonl # Session messages agents/<agent_id>/agent/auth-profiles.json # API keys

Computational neuroscience: Hodgkin-Huxley conductances, Leaky Integrate-and-Fire dynamics, and the underlying membrane biophysics (Nernst equilibrium, Goldman-Hodgkin-Katz, passive cable constants).

# lexopt 0.3.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/lexopt/0.3.2

# Lexopt

Lexopt is an argument parser for Rust. It tries to have the simplest possible design that's still correct. It's so simple that it's a bit tedious to use.

Lexopt is:

- Small: one file, no dependencies, no macros. Easy to audit or vendor.
- Correct: standard conventions are supported and ambiguity is avoided. Tested and fuzzed.
- Pedantic: arguments are returned as `OsString`
- Imperative: options are returned as they are found, nothing is declared ahead of time.
- Minimalist: only basic functionality is provided.
- Unhelpful: there is no help generation and error messages often lack context.

## Example

```
```
Let's walk through this:

- We start parsing with `Parser::from_env()`.
- We call `parser.next()`in a loop to get all the arguments until they run out.
- We match on arguments. `Short`and`Long`indicate an option.
- To get the value that belongs to an option (like `10`in`-n 10`) we call`parser.value()`.- This returns a standard `OsString`- For convenience, `use lexopt::prelude::*`adds a`.parse()`method, analogous to[the one on](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.str.html#method.parse).`&str`

- For convenience,
- Calling `parser.value()`is how we tell`Parser`that`-n`takes a value at all.

- This returns a standard
- `Value`indicates a free-standing argument.- `if thing.is_none()`is a useful pattern for positional arguments. If we already found- `thing`we pass it on to another case.
- It also contains an `OsString`.- The `.string()`method decodes it into a plain`String`.

- The

- If we don't know what to do with an argument we use `return Err(arg.unexpected())`to turn it into an error message.
- Strings can be promoted to errors for custom error messages.

This covers most of the functionality in the library. Lexopt does very little for you.

For a larger example with useful patterns, see [ examples/cargo.rs](https://docs.rs/examples/cargo.rs).

## Command line syntax

The following conventions are supported:

- Short options (`-q`)
- Long options (`--verbose`)
- `--`to mark the end of options
- `=`to separate options from values (- `--option=value`,- `-o=value`)- The nonstandard `-o=value`syntax can be[disabled](https://docs.rs/lexopt/latest/lexopt/struct.Parser.html#method.set_short_equals).

- The nonstandard
- Spaces to separate options from values (`--option value`,`-o value`)
- Unseparated short options (`-ovalue`)
- Combined short options (`-abc`to mean`-a -b -c`)
- Options with optional arguments (like GNU sed's `-i`, which can be used standalone or as`-iSUFFIX`) (`Parser::optional_value()`
- Options with multiple arguments (`Parser::values()`

These are not supported out of the box:

- Single-dash long options (like find's `-name`)
- Abbreviated long options (GNU's getopt lets you write `--num`instead of`--number`if it can be expanded unambiguously)

[ Parser::raw_args()](https://docs.rs/lexopt/latest/lexopt/struct.Parser.html#method.raw_args) and

[provide an escape hatch for consuming the original command line. This can be used for custom syntax, like treating](https://docs.rs/lexopt/latest/lexopt/struct.Parser.html#method.try_raw_args)

`Parser::try_raw_args()``-123` as a number instead of a string of options. See [for an example of this.](https://docs.rs/examples/nonstandard.rs)

`examples/nonstandard.rs`## Unicode

This library supports unicode while tolerating non-unicode arguments.

Short options may be unicode, but only a single codepoint (a `char`).

Options can be combined with non-unicode arguments. That is, `--option=���` will not cause an error or mangle the value.

Options themselves are patched as by [ String::from_utf8_lossy](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/string/struct.String.html#method.from_utf8_lossy) if they're not valid unicode. That typically means you'll raise an error later when they're not recognized.

## Why?

For a particular application I was looking for a small parser that's pedantically correct. There are other compact argument parsing libraries, but I couldn't find one that handled `OsString`s and implemented all the fiddly details of the argument syntax faithfully.

This library may also be useful if a lot of control is desired, like when the exact argument order matters or not all options are known ahead of time. It could be considered more of a lexer than a parser.

## Why not?

This library may not be worth using if:

- You don't care about non-unicode arguments
- You don't care about exact compliance and correctness
- You don't care about code size
- You do care about great error messages
- You hate boilerplate

## See also

- [Collected benchmarks of argument parsing crates](https://github.com/rosetta-rs/argparse-rosetta-rs).
- libc's `getopt`
- Plan 9's *arg(3)*macros

---

# lexopt - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/lexopt/0.3.2/target-redirect/lexopt/

## Expand description

A pathologically simple command line argument parser.

Most argument parsers are declarative: you tell them what to parse, and they do it.

This one provides you with a stream of options and values and lets you figure out the rest.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
struct Args {
    thing: String,
    number: u32,
    shout: bool,
}
fn parse_args() -> Result<Args, lexopt::Error> {
    use lexopt::prelude::*;
    let mut thing = None;
    let mut number = 1;
    let mut shout = false;
    let mut parser = lexopt::Parser::from_env();
    while let Some(arg) = parser.next()? {
        match arg {
            Short('n') | Long("number") => {
                number = parser.value()?.parse()?;
            }
            Long("shout") => {
                shout = true;
            }
            Value(val) if thing.is_none() => {
                thing = Some(val.string()?);
            }
            Long("help") => {
                println!("Usage: hello [-n|--number=NUM] [--shout] THING");
                std::process::exit(0);
            }
            _ => return Err(arg.unexpected()),
        }
    }
    Ok(Args {
        thing: thing.ok_or("missing argument THING")?,
        number,
        shout,
    })
}
fn main() -> Result<(), lexopt::Error> {
    let args = parse_args()?;
    let mut message = format!("Hello {}", args.thing);
    if args.shout {
        message = message.to_uppercase();
    }
    for _ in 0..args.number {
        println!("{}", message);
    }
    Ok(())
}
```
Let’s walk through this:

- We start parsing with `Parser::from_env`
- We call `parser.next()`
- We match on arguments. `Short``Long`
- To get the value that belongs to an option (like `10`in`-n 10`) we call`parser.value()`- This returns a standard `OsString`
- For convenience, `use lexopt::prelude::*``.parse()``str::parse`
- Calling `parser.value()`is how we tell`Parser`that`-n`takes a value at all.

- This returns a standard
- `Value`indicates a free-standing argument.- `if thing.is_none()`is a useful pattern for positional arguments. If we already found- `thing`we pass it on to another case.
- It also contains an `OsString`.- The `.string()``String`.

- The

- If we don’t know what to do with an argument we use `return Err(arg.unexpected())`
- Strings can be promoted to errors for custom error messages.

- A small prelude for processing arguments.

[152](https://docs.rs#152)impl Parser {
[153](https://docs.rs#153)    /// Get the next option or positional argument.
[154](https://docs.rs#154)    ///
[155](https://docs.rs#155)    /// A return value of `Ok(None)` means the command line has been exhausted.
[156](https://docs.rs#156)    ///
[157](https://docs.rs#157)    /// Options that are not valid unicode are transformed with replacement
[158](https://docs.rs#158)    /// characters as by [`String::from_utf8_lossy`].
[159](https://docs.rs#159)    ///
[160](https://docs.rs#160)    /// # Errors
[161](https://docs.rs#161)    ///
[162](https://docs.rs#162)    /// [`Error::UnexpectedValue`] is returned if the last option had a
[163](https://docs.rs#163)    /// value that hasn't been consumed, as in `--option=value` or `-o=value`.
[164](https://docs.rs#164)    ///
[165](https://docs.rs#165)    /// It's possible to continue parsing after an error (but this is rarely useful).
[166](https://docs.rs#166)    pub fn next(&mut self) -> Result<Option<Arg<'_>>, Error> {
[167](https://docs.rs#167)        match self.state {
[168](https://docs.rs#168)            State::PendingValue(ref mut value) => {
[169](https://docs.rs#169)                // Last time we got `--long=value`, and `value` hasn't been used.
[170](https://docs.rs#170)                let value = replace(value, OsString::new());
[171](https://docs.rs#171)                self.state = State::None;
[172](https://docs.rs#172)                return Err(Error::UnexpectedValue {
[173](https://docs.rs#173)                    option: self
[174](https://docs.rs#174)                        .format_last_option()
[175](https://docs.rs#175)                        .expect("Should only have pending value after long option"),
[176](https://docs.rs#176)                    value,
[177](https://docs.rs#177)                });
[178](https://docs.rs#178)            }
[179](https://docs.rs#179)            State::Shorts(ref arg, ref mut pos) => {
[180](https://docs.rs#180)                // We're somewhere inside a -abc chain. Because we're in .next(),
[181](https://docs.rs#181)                // not .value(), we can assume that the next character is another option.
[182](https://docs.rs#182)                match first_codepoint(&arg[*pos..]) {
[183](https://docs.rs#183)                    Ok(None) => {
[184](https://docs.rs#184)                        self.state = State::None;
[185](https://docs.rs#185)                    }
[186](https://docs.rs#186)                    // If we find "-=[...]" we interpret it as an option.
[187](https://docs.rs#187)                    // If we find "-o=..." then there's an unexpected value.
[188](https://docs.rs#188)                    // ('-=' as an option exists, see https://linux.die.net/man/1/a2ps.
[189](https://docs.rs#189)                    // Though if you have one you should maybe disable short_equals.)
[190](https://docs.rs#190)                    // clap always interprets it as a short flag in this case, but
[191](https://docs.rs#191)                    // that feels sloppy.
[192](https://docs.rs#192)                    Ok(Some('=')) if *pos > 1 && self.short_equals => {
[193](https://docs.rs#193)                        return Err(Error::UnexpectedValue {
[194](https://docs.rs#194)                            option: self.format_last_option().unwrap(),
[195](https://docs.rs#195)                            value: self.optional_value().unwrap(),
[196](https://docs.rs#196)                        });
[197](https://docs.rs#197)                    }
[198](https://docs.rs#198)                    Ok(Some(ch)) => {
[199](https://docs.rs#199)                        *pos += ch.len_utf8();
[200](https://docs.rs#200)                        self.last_option = LastOption::Short(ch);
[201](https://docs.rs#201)                        return Ok(Some(Arg::Short(ch)));
[202](https://docs.rs#202)                    }
[203](https://docs.rs#203)                    Err(err) => {
[204](https://docs.rs#204)                        // Advancing may allow recovery.
[205](https://docs.rs#205)                        // This is a little iffy, there might be more bad unicode next.
[206](https://docs.rs#206)                        match err.error_len() {
[207](https://docs.rs#207)                            Some(len) => *pos += len,
[208](https://docs.rs#208)                            None => *pos = arg.len(),
[209](https://docs.rs#209)                        }
[210](https://docs.rs#210)                        self.last_option = LastOption::Short('�');
[211](https://docs.rs#211)                        return Ok(Some(Arg::Short('�')));
[212](https://docs.rs#212)                    }
[213](https://docs.rs#213)                }
[214](https://docs.rs#214)            }
[215](https://docs.rs#215)            #[cfg(windows)]
[216](https://docs.rs#216)            State::ShortsU16(ref arg, ref mut pos) => match first_utf16_codepoint(&arg[*pos..]) {
[217](https://docs.rs#217)                Ok(None) => {
[218](https://docs.rs#218)                    self.state = State::None;
[219](https://docs.rs#219)                }
[220](https://docs.rs#220)                Ok(Some('=')) if *pos > 1 && self.short_equals => {
[221](https://docs.rs#221)                    return Err(Error::UnexpectedValue {
[222](https://docs.rs#222)                        option: self.format_last_option().unwrap(),
[223](https://docs.rs#223)                        value: self.optional_value().unwrap(),
[224](https://docs.rs#224)                    });
[225](https://docs.rs#225)                }
[226](https://docs.rs#226)                Ok(Some(ch)) => {
[227](https://docs.rs#227)                    *pos += ch.len_utf16();
[228](https://docs.rs#228)                    self.last_option = LastOption::Short(ch);
[229](https://docs.rs#229)                    return Ok(Some(Arg::Short(ch)));
[230](https://docs.rs#230)                }
[231](https://docs.rs#231)                Err(_) => {
[232](https://docs.rs#232)                    *pos += 1;
[233](https://docs.rs#233)                    self.last_option = LastOption::Short('�');
[234](https://docs.rs#234)                    return Ok(Some(Arg::Short('�')));
[235](https://docs.rs#235)                }
[236](https://docs.rs#236)            },
[237](https://docs.rs#237)            State::FinishedOpts => {
[238](https://docs.rs#238)                return Ok(self.source.next().map(Arg::Value));
[239](https://docs.rs#239)            }
[240](https://docs.rs#240)            State::None => (),
[241](https://docs.rs#241)        }
[242](https://docs.rs#242)
[243](https://docs.rs#243)        match self.state {
[244](https://docs.rs#244)            State::None => (),
[245](https://docs.rs#245)            ref state => panic!("unexpected state {:?}", state),
[246](https://docs.rs#246)        }
[247](https://docs.rs#247)
[248](https://docs.rs#248)        let arg = match self.source.next() {
[249](https://docs.rs#249)            Some(arg) => arg,
[250](https://docs.rs#250)            None => return Ok(None),
[251](https://docs.rs#251)        };
[252](https://docs.rs#252)
[253](https://docs.rs#253)        if arg == "--" {
[254](https://docs.rs#254)            self.state = State::FinishedOpts;
[255](https://docs.rs#255)            return self.next();
[256](https://docs.rs#256)        }
[257](https://docs.rs#257)
[258](https://docs.rs#258)        #[cfg(unix)]
[259](https://docs.rs#259)        {
[260](https://docs.rs#260)            // Fast solution for platforms where OsStrings are just UTF-8-ish bytes
[261](https://docs.rs#261)            let mut arg = arg.into_vec();
[262](https://docs.rs#262)            if arg.starts_with(b"--") {
[263](https://docs.rs#263)                // Long options have two forms: --option and --option=value.
[264](https://docs.rs#264)                if let Some(ind) = arg.iter().position(|&b| b == b'=') {
[265](https://docs.rs#265)                    // The value can be an OsString...
[266](https://docs.rs#266)                    self.state = State::PendingValue(OsString::from_vec(arg[ind + 1..].into()));
[267](https://docs.rs#267)                    arg.truncate(ind);
[268](https://docs.rs#268)                }
[269](https://docs.rs#269)                // ...but the option has to be a string.
[270](https://docs.rs#270)                // String::from_utf8_lossy().into_owned() would work, but its
[271](https://docs.rs#271)                // return type is Cow: if the original was valid a borrowed
[272](https://docs.rs#272)                // version is returned, and then into_owned() does an
[273](https://docs.rs#273)                // unnecessary copy.
[274](https://docs.rs#274)                // By trying String::from_utf8 first we avoid that copy if arg
[275](https://docs.rs#275)                // is already UTF-8 (which is most of the time).
[276](https://docs.rs#276)                // reqwest does a similar maneuver more efficiently with unsafe:
[277](https://docs.rs#277)                // https://github.com/seanmonstar/reqwest/blob/e6a1a09f0904e06de4ff1317278798c4ed28af66/src/async_impl/response.rs#L194
[278](https://docs.rs#278)                let option = match String::from_utf8(arg) {
[279](https://docs.rs#279)                    Ok(text) => text,
[280](https://docs.rs#280)                    Err(err) => String::from_utf8_lossy(err.as_bytes()).into_owned(),
[281](https://docs.rs#281)                };
[282](https://docs.rs#282)                Ok(Some(self.set_long(option)))
[283](https://docs.rs#283)            } else if arg.len() > 1 && arg[0] == b'-' {
[284](https://docs.rs#284)                self.state = State::Shorts(arg, 1);
[285](https://docs.rs#285)                self.next()
[286](https://docs.rs#286)            } else {
[287](https://docs.rs#287)                Ok(Some(Arg::Value(OsString::from_vec(arg))))
[288](https://docs.rs#288)            }
[289](https://docs.rs#289)        }
[290](https://docs.rs#290)
[291](https://docs.rs#291)        #[cfg(not(unix))]
[292](https://docs.rs#292)        {
[293](https://docs.rs#293)            // Platforms where looking inside an OsString is harder
[294](https://docs.rs#294)
[295](https://docs.rs#295)            #[cfg(windows)]
[296](https://docs.rs#296)            {
[297](https://docs.rs#297)                // Fast path for Windows
[298](https://docs.rs#298)                let mut bytes = arg.encode_wide();
[299](https://docs.rs#299)                const DASH: u16 = b'-' as u16;
[300](https://docs.rs#300)                match (bytes.next(), bytes.next()) {
[301](https://docs.rs#301)                    (Some(DASH), Some(_)) => {
[302](https://docs.rs#302)                        // This is an option, we'll have to do more work.
[303](https://docs.rs#303)                        // (We already checked for "--" earlier.)
[304](https://docs.rs#304)                    }
[305](https://docs.rs#305)                    _ => {
[306](https://docs.rs#306)                        // Just a value, return early.
[307](https://docs.rs#307)                        return Ok(Some(Arg::Value(arg)));
[308](https://docs.rs#308)                    }
[309](https://docs.rs#309)                }
[310](https://docs.rs#310)            }
[311](https://docs.rs#311)
[312](https://docs.rs#312)            let mut arg = match arg.into_string() {
[313](https://docs.rs#313)                Ok(arg) => arg,
[314](https://docs.rs#314)                Err(arg) => {
[315](https://docs.rs#315)                    // The argument is not valid unicode.
[316](https://docs.rs#316)                    // If it's an option we'll have to do something nasty,
[317](https://docs.rs#317)                    // otherwise we can return it as-is.
[318](https://docs.rs#318)
[319](https://docs.rs#319)                    #[cfg(windows)]
[320](https://docs.rs#320)                    {
[321](https://docs.rs#321)                        // On Windows we can only get here if this is an option, otherwise
[322](https://docs.rs#322)                        // we return earlier.
[323](https://docs.rs#323)                        // Unlike on Unix, we can't efficiently process invalid unicode.
[324](https://docs.rs#324)                        // Semantically it's UTF-16, but internally it's WTF-8 (a superset of UTF-8).
[325](https://docs.rs#325)                        // So we only process the raw version here, when we know we really have to.
[326](https://docs.rs#326)                        let mut arg: Vec<u16> = arg.encode_wide().collect();
[327](https://docs.rs#327)                        const DASH: u16 = b'-' as u16;
[328](https://docs.rs#328)                        const EQ: u16 = b'=' as u16;
[329](https://docs.rs#329)                        if arg.starts_with(&[DASH, DASH]) {
[330](https://docs.rs#330)                            if let Some(ind) = arg.iter().position(|&u| u == EQ) {
[331](https://docs.rs#331)                                self.state =
[332](https://docs.rs#332)                                    State::PendingValue(OsString::from_wide(&arg[ind + 1..]));
[333](https://docs.rs#333)                                arg.truncate(ind);
[334](https://docs.rs#334)                            }
[335](https://docs.rs#335)                            let long = self.set_long(String::from_utf16_lossy(&arg));
[336](https://docs.rs#336)                            return Ok(Some(long));
[337](https://docs.rs#337)                        } else {
[338](https://docs.rs#338)                            assert!(arg.len() > 1);
[339](https://docs.rs#339)                            assert_eq!(arg[0], DASH);
[340](https://docs.rs#340)                            self.state = State::ShortsU16(arg, 1);
[341](https://docs.rs#341)                            return self.next();
[342](https://docs.rs#342)                        }
[343](https://docs.rs#343)                    };
[344](https://docs.rs#344)
[345](https://docs.rs#345)                    #[cfg(not(windows))]
[346](https://docs.rs#346)                    {
[347](https://docs.rs#347)                        // Other platforms.
[348](https://docs.rs#348)
[349](https://docs.rs#349)                        // Most of them have their own `OsStrExt` but that doesn't mean
[350](https://docs.rs#350)                        // they actually have invalid strings. WASI for example exports
[351](https://docs.rs#351)                        // the Unix extension trait even though only UTF-8 OS strings
[352](https://docs.rs#352)                        // are allowed.
[353](https://docs.rs#353)                        // So on WASI this code path is only reachable by creating custom
[354](https://docs.rs#354)                        // faulty OS strings, not by processing true environment args.
[355](https://docs.rs#355)
[356](https://docs.rs#356)                        // This allocates unconditionally, sadly.
[357](https://docs.rs#357)                        let text = arg.to_string_lossy();
[358](https://docs.rs#358)                        if text.starts_with('-') {
[359](https://docs.rs#359)                            // Use the lossily patched version and hope for the best.
[360](https://docs.rs#360)                            // This may be incorrect behavior.
[361](https://docs.rs#361)                            // Other options are returning an error or (as of Rust 1.74)
[362](https://docs.rs#362)                            // using the unsafe encoded_bytes API. But neither seem worth
[363](https://docs.rs#363)                            // it in this obscure corner, especially since they'd be hard
[364](https://docs.rs#364)                            // to test.
[365](https://docs.rs#365)                            // (The entire crate will most likely move to the encoded_bytes
[366](https://docs.rs#366)                            // API in the future, once it supports checked conversion.)
[367](https://docs.rs#367)                            // Please open an issue if this behavior affects you!
[368](https://docs.rs#368)                            text.into_owned()
[369](https://docs.rs#369)                        } else {
[370](https://docs.rs#370)                            // It didn't look like an option, so return it as a value.
[371](https://docs.rs#371)                            return Ok(Some(Arg::Value(arg)));
[372](https://docs.rs#372)                        }
[373](https://docs.rs#373)                    }
[374](https://docs.rs#374)                }
[375](https://docs.rs#375)            };
[376](https://docs.rs#376)
[377](https://docs.rs#377)            // The argument is valid unicode. This is the ideal version of the
[378](https://docs.rs#378)            // code, the previous mess was purely to deal with invalid unicode.
[379](https://docs.rs#379)            if arg.starts_with("--") {
[380](https://docs.rs#380)                if let Some(ind) = arg.find('=') {
[381](https://docs.rs#381)                    self.state = State::PendingValue(arg[ind + 1..].into());
[382](https://docs.rs#382)                    arg.truncate(ind);
[383](https://docs.rs#383)                }
[384](https://docs.rs#384)                Ok(Some(self.set_long(arg)))
[385](https://docs.rs#385)            } else if arg.starts_with('-') && arg != "-" {
[386](https://docs.rs#386)                self.state = State::Shorts(arg.into(), 1);
[387](https://docs.rs#387)                self.next()
[388](https://docs.rs#388)            } else {
[389](https://docs.rs#389)                Ok(Some(Arg::Value(arg.into())))
[390](https://docs.rs#390)            }
[391](https://docs.rs#391)        }
[392](https://docs.rs#392)    }
[393](https://docs.rs#393)
[394](https://docs.rs#394)    /// Get a value for an option.
[395](https://docs.rs#395)    ///
[396](https://docs.rs#396)    /// This function should normally be called right after seeing an option
[397](https://docs.rs#397)    /// that expects a value, with positional arguments being collected
[398](https://docs.rs#398)    /// using [`next()`][Parser::next].
[399](https://docs.rs#399)    ///
[400](https://docs.rs#400)    /// A value is collected even if it looks like an option
[401](https://docs.rs#401)    /// (i.e., starts with `-`).
[402](https://docs.rs#402)    ///
[403](https://docs.rs#403)    /// # Errors
[404](https://docs.rs#404)    ///
[405](https://docs.rs#405)    /// An [`Error::MissingValue`] is returned if the end of the command
[406](https://docs.rs#406)    /// line is reached.
[407](https://docs.rs#407)    pub fn value(&mut self) -> Result<OsString, Error> {
[408](https://docs.rs#408)        if let Some(value) = self.optional_value() {
[409](https://docs.rs#409)            return Ok(value);
[410](https://docs.rs#410)        }
[411](https://docs.rs#411)
[412](https://docs.rs#412)        if let Some(value) = self.source.next() {
[413](https://docs.rs#413)            return Ok(value);
[414](https://docs.rs#414)        }
[415](https://docs.rs#415)
[416](https://docs.rs#416)        Err(Error::MissingValue {
[417](https://docs.rs#417)            option: self.format_last_option(),
[418](https://docs.rs#418)        })
[419](https://docs.rs#419)    }
[420](https://docs.rs#420)
[421](https://docs.rs#421)    /// Gather multiple values for an option.
[422](https://docs.rs#422)    ///
[423](https://docs.rs#423)    /// This is used for options that take multiple arguments, such as a
[424](https://docs.rs#424)    /// `--command` flag that's invoked as `app --command echo 'Hello world'`.
[425](https://docs.rs#425)    ///
[426](https://docs.rs#426)    /// It will gather arguments until another option is found, or `--` is found, or
[427](https://docs.rs#427)    /// the end of the command line is reached. This differs from `.value()`, which
[428](https://docs.rs#428)    /// takes a value even if it looks like an option.
[429](https://docs.rs#429)    ///
[430](https://docs.rs#430)    /// On success the resulting iterator will yield at least one value.
[431](https://docs.rs#431)    ///
[432](https://docs.rs#432)    /// An equals sign (`=`) will limit this to a single value. That means `-a=b c` and
[433](https://docs.rs#433)    /// `--opt=b c` will only yield `"b"` while `-a b c`, `-ab c` and `--opt b c` will
[434](https://docs.rs#434)    /// yield `"b"`, `"c"`.
[435](https://docs.rs#435)    ///
[436](https://docs.rs#436)    /// (If [`short_equals`](Self::set_short_equals) is disabled then `-a=b c` will yield
[437](https://docs.rs#437)    /// `"=b"`, `"c"`.)
[438](https://docs.rs#438)    ///
[439](https://docs.rs#439)    /// # Errors
[440](https://docs.rs#440)    /// If not at least one value is found then [`Error::MissingValue`] is returned.
[441](https://docs.rs#441)    ///
[442](https://docs.rs#442)    /// # Example
[443](https://docs.rs#443)    /// ```
[444](https://docs.rs#444)    /// # fn main() -> Result<(), lexopt::Error> {
[445](https://docs.rs#445)    /// # use lexopt::prelude::*;
[446](https://docs.rs#446)    /// # use std::ffi::OsString;
[447](https://docs.rs#447)    /// # use std::path::PathBuf;
[448](https://docs.rs#448)    /// # let mut parser = lexopt::Parser::from_args(&["a", "b", "-x", "one", "two", "three", "four"]);
[449](https://docs.rs#449)    /// let arguments: Vec<OsString> = parser.values()?.collect();
[450](https://docs.rs#450)    /// # assert_eq!(arguments, &["a", "b"]);
[451](https://docs.rs#451)    /// # let _ = parser.next();
[452](https://docs.rs#452)    /// let at_most_three_files: Vec<PathBuf> = parser.values()?.take(3).map(Into::into).collect();
[453](https://docs.rs#453)    /// # assert_eq!(parser.raw_args()?.as_slice(), &["four"]);
[454](https://docs.rs#454)    /// for value in parser.values()? {
[455](https://docs.rs#455)    ///     // ...
[456](https://docs.rs#456)    /// }
[457](https://docs.rs#457)    /// # Ok(()) }
[458](https://docs.rs#458)    /// ```
[459](https://docs.rs#459)    pub fn values(&mut self) -> Result<ValuesIter<'_>, Error> {
[460](https://docs.rs#460)        // This code is designed so that just calling .values() doesn't consume
[461](https://docs.rs#461)        // any arguments as long as you don't use the iterator. It used to work
[462](https://docs.rs#462)        // differently.
[463](https://docs.rs#463)        // "--" is treated like an option and not consumed. This seems to me the
[464](https://docs.rs#464)        // least unreasonable behavior, and it's the easiest to implement.
[465](https://docs.rs#465)        if self.has_pending() || self.next_is_normal() {
[466](https://docs.rs#466)            Ok(ValuesIter {
[467](https://docs.rs#467)                took_first: false,
[468](https://docs.rs#468)                parser: Some(self),
[469](https://docs.rs#469)            })
[470](https://docs.rs#470)        } else {
[471](https://docs.rs#471)            Err(Error::MissingValue {
[472](https://docs.rs#472)                option: self.format_last_option(),
[473](https://docs.rs#473)            })
[474](https://docs.rs#474)        }
[475](https://docs.rs#475)    }
[476](https://docs.rs#476)
[477](https://docs.rs#477)    /// Inspect an argument and consume it if it's "normal" (not an option or --).
[478](https://docs.rs#478)    ///
[479](https://docs.rs#479)    /// Used by [`Parser::values`].
[480](https://docs.rs#480)    ///
[481](https://docs.rs#481)    /// This method should not be called while partway through processing an
[482](https://docs.rs#482)    /// argument.
[483](https://docs.rs#483)    fn next_if_normal(&mut self) -> Option<OsString> {
[484](https://docs.rs#484)        if self.next_is_normal() {
[485](https://docs.rs#485)            self.source.next()
[486](https://docs.rs#486)        } else {
[487](https://docs.rs#487)            None
[488](https://docs.rs#488)        }
[489](https://docs.rs#489)    }
[490](https://docs.rs#490)
[491](https://docs.rs#491)    /// Execute the check for next_if_normal().
[492](https://docs.rs#492)    fn next_is_normal(&self) -> bool {
[493](https://docs.rs#493)        assert!(!self.has_pending());
[494](https://docs.rs#494)        let arg = match self.source.as_slice().first() {
[495](https://docs.rs#495)            // There has to be a next argument.
[496](https://docs.rs#496)            None => return false,
[497](https://docs.rs#497)            Some(arg) => arg,
[498](https://docs.rs#498)        };
[499](https://docs.rs#499)        if let State::FinishedOpts = self.state {
[500](https://docs.rs#500)            // If we already found a -- then we're really not supposed to be here,
[501](https://docs.rs#501)            // but we shouldn't treat the next argument as an option.
[502](https://docs.rs#502)            return true;
[503](https://docs.rs#503)        }
[504](https://docs.rs#504)        if arg == "-" {
[505](https://docs.rs#505)            // "-" is the one argument with a leading '-' that's allowed.
[506](https://docs.rs#506)            return true;
[507](https://docs.rs#507)        }
[508](https://docs.rs#508)        #[cfg(unix)]
[509](https://docs.rs#509)        let lead_dash = arg.as_bytes().first() == Some(&b'-');
[510](https://docs.rs#510)        #[cfg(windows)]
[511](https://docs.rs#511)        let lead_dash = arg.encode_wide().next() == Some(b'-' as u16);
[512](https://docs.rs#512)        #[cfg(not(any(unix, windows)))]
[513](https://docs.rs#513)        let lead_dash = arg.to_string_lossy().as_bytes().first() == Some(&b'-');
[514](https://docs.rs#514)
[515](https://docs.rs#515)        !lead_dash
[516](https://docs.rs#516)    }
[517](https://docs.rs#517)
[518](https://docs.rs#518)    /// Take raw arguments from the original command line.
[519](https://docs.rs#519)    ///
[520](https://docs.rs#520)    /// This returns an iterator of [`OsString`]s. Any arguments that are not
[521](https://docs.rs#521)    /// consumed are kept, so you can continue parsing after you're done with
[522](https://docs.rs#522)    /// the iterator.
[523](https://docs.rs#523)    ///
[524](https://docs.rs#524)    /// To inspect an argument without consuming it, use [`RawArgs::peek`] or
[525](https://docs.rs#525)    /// [`RawArgs::as_slice`].
[526](https://docs.rs#526)    ///
[527](https://docs.rs#527)    /// # Errors
[528](https://docs.rs#528)    ///
[529](https://docs.rs#529)    /// Returns an [`Error::UnexpectedValue`] if the last option had a left-over
[530](https://docs.rs#530)    /// argument, as in `--option=value`, `-ovalue`, or if it was midway through
[531](https://docs.rs#531)    /// an option chain, as in `-abc`. The iterator only yields whole arguments.
[532](https://docs.rs#532)    /// To avoid this, use [`try_raw_args()`][Parser::try_raw_args].
[533](https://docs.rs#533)    ///
[534](https://docs.rs#534)    /// After this error the method is guaranteed to succeed, as it consumes the
[535](https://docs.rs#535)    /// rest of the argument.
[536](https://docs.rs#536)    ///
[537](https://docs.rs#537)    /// # Example
[538](https://docs.rs#538)    /// As soon as a free-standing argument is found, consume the other arguments
[539](https://docs.rs#539)    /// as-is, and build them into a command.
[540](https://docs.rs#540)    /// ```
[541](https://docs.rs#541)    /// # fn main() -> Result<(), lexopt::Error> {
[542](https://docs.rs#542)    /// # use lexopt::prelude::*;
[543](https://docs.rs#543)    /// # use std::ffi::OsString;
[544](https://docs.rs#544)    /// # use std::path::PathBuf;
[545](https://docs.rs#545)    /// # let mut parser = lexopt::Parser::from_args(&["-x", "echo", "-n", "'Hello, world'"]);
[546](https://docs.rs#546)    /// # while let Some(arg) = parser.next()? {
[547](https://docs.rs#547)    /// # match arg {
[548](https://docs.rs#548)    /// Value(prog) => {
[549](https://docs.rs#549)    ///     let args: Vec<_> = parser.raw_args()?.collect();
[550](https://docs.rs#550)    ///     let command = std::process::Command::new(prog).args(args);
[551](https://docs.rs#551)    /// }
[552](https://docs.rs#552)    /// # _ => (), }} Ok(()) }
[553](https://docs.rs#553)    /// ```
[554](https://docs.rs#554)    pub fn raw_args(&mut self) -> Result<RawArgs<'_>, Error> {
[555](https://docs.rs#555)        if let Some(value) = self.optional_value() {
[556](https://docs.rs#556)            return Err(Error::UnexpectedValue {
[557](https://docs.rs#557)                option: self.format_last_option().unwrap(),
[558](https://docs.rs#558)                value,
[559](https://docs.rs#559)            });
[560](https://docs.rs#560)        }
[561](https://docs.rs#561)
[562](https://docs.rs#562)        Ok(RawArgs(&mut self.source))
[563](https://docs.rs#563)    }
[564](https://docs.rs#564)
[565](https://docs.rs#565)    /// Take raw arguments from the original command line, *if* the current argument
[566](https://docs.rs#566)    /// has finished processing.
[567](https://docs.rs#567)    ///
[568](https://docs.rs#568)    /// Unlike [`raw_args()`][Parser::raw_args] this does not consume any value
[569](https://docs.rs#569)    /// in case of a left-over argument. This makes it safe to call at any time.
[570](https://docs.rs#570)    ///
[571](https://docs.rs#571)    /// It returns `None` exactly when [`optional_value()`][Parser::optional_value]
[572](https://docs.rs#572)    /// would return `Some`.
[573](https://docs.rs#573)    ///
[574](https://docs.rs#574)    /// Note: If no arguments are left then it returns an empty iterator (not `None`).
[575](https://docs.rs#575)    ///
[576](https://docs.rs#576)    /// # Example
[577](https://docs.rs#577)    /// Process arguments of the form `-123` as numbers. For a complete runnable version of
[578](https://docs.rs#578)    /// this example, see
[579](https://docs.rs#579)    /// [`examples/nonstandard.rs`](https://github.com/blyxxyz/lexopt/blob/e3754e6f24506afb42394602fc257b1ad9258d84/examples/nonstandard.rs).
[580](https://docs.rs#580)    /// ```
[581](https://docs.rs#581)    /// # fn main() -> Result<(), lexopt::Error> {
[582](https://docs.rs#582)    /// # use lexopt::prelude::*;
[583](https://docs.rs#583)    /// # use std::ffi::OsString;
[584](https://docs.rs#584)    /// # use std::path::PathBuf;
[585](https://docs.rs#585)    /// # let mut parser = lexopt::Parser::from_iter(&["-13"]);
[586](https://docs.rs#586)    /// fn parse_dashnum(parser: &mut lexopt::Parser) -> Option<u64> {
[587](https://docs.rs#587)    ///     let mut raw = parser.try_raw_args()?;
[588](https://docs.rs#588)    ///     let arg = raw.peek()?.to_str()?;
[589](https://docs.rs#589)    ///     let num = arg.strip_prefix('-')?.parse::<u64>().ok()?;
[590](https://docs.rs#590)    ///     raw.next(); // Consume the argument we just parsed
[591](https://docs.rs#591)    ///     Some(num)
[592](https://docs.rs#592)    /// }
[593](https://docs.rs#593)    ///
[594](https://docs.rs#594)    /// loop {
[595](https://docs.rs#595)    ///     if let Some(num) = parse_dashnum(&mut parser) {
[596](https://docs.rs#596)    ///         println!("Got number {}", num);
[597](https://docs.rs#597)    ///     } else if let Some(arg) = parser.next()? {
[598](https://docs.rs#598)    ///         match arg {
[599](https://docs.rs#599)    ///             // ...
[600](https://docs.rs#600)    ///             # _ => (),
[601](https://docs.rs#601)    ///         }
[602](https://docs.rs#602)    ///     } else {
[603](https://docs.rs#603)    ///         break;
[604](https://docs.rs#604)    ///     }
[605](https://docs.rs#605)    /// }
[606](https://docs.rs#606)    /// # Ok(()) }
[607](https://docs.rs#607)    /// ```
[608](https://docs.rs#608)    pub fn try_raw_args(&mut self) -> Option<RawArgs<'_>> {
[609](https://docs.rs#609)        if self.has_pending() {
[610](https://docs.rs#610)            None
[611](https://docs.rs#611)        } else {
[612](https://docs.rs#612)            Some(RawArgs(&mut self.source))
[613](https://docs.rs#613)        }
[614](https://docs.rs#614)    }
[615](https://docs.rs#615)
[616](https://docs.rs#616)    /// Check whether we're halfway through an argument, or in other words,
[617](https://docs.rs#617)    /// if [`Parser::optional_value()`] would return `Some`.
[618](https://docs.rs#618)    fn has_pending(&self) -> bool {
[619](https://docs.rs#619)        match self.state {
[620](https://docs.rs#620)            State::None | State::FinishedOpts => false,
[621](https://docs.rs#621)            State::PendingValue(_) => true,
[622](https://docs.rs#622)            State::Shorts(ref arg, pos) => pos < arg.len(),
[623](https://docs.rs#623)            #[cfg(windows)]
[624](https://docs.rs#624)            State::ShortsU16(ref arg, pos) => pos < arg.len(),
[625](https://docs.rs#625)        }
[626](https://docs.rs#626)    }
[627](https://docs.rs#627)
[628](https://docs.rs#628)    #[inline(never)]
[629](https://docs.rs#629)    fn format_last_option(&self) -> Option<String> {
[630](https://docs.rs#630)        match self.last_option {
[631](https://docs.rs#631)            LastOption::None => None,
[632](https://docs.rs#632)            LastOption::Short(ch) => Some(format!("-{}", ch)),
[633](https://docs.rs#633)            LastOption::Long(ref option) => Some(option.clone()),
[634](https://docs.rs#634)        }
[635](https://docs.rs#635)    }

[637](https://docs.rs#637)    /// The name of the command, as in the zeroth argument of the process.
[638](https://docs.rs#638)    ///
[639](https://docs.rs#639)    /// This is intended for use in messages. If the name is not valid unicode
[640](https://docs.rs#640)    /// it will be sanitized with replacement characters as by
[641](https://docs.rs#641)    /// [`String::from_utf8_lossy`].
[642](https://docs.rs#642)    ///
[643](https://docs.rs#643)    /// To get the current executable, use [`std::env::current_exe`].
[644](https://docs.rs#644)    ///
[645](https://docs.rs#645)    /// # Example
[646](https://docs.rs#646)    /// ```
[647](https://docs.rs#647)    /// let mut parser = lexopt::Parser::from_env();
[648](https://docs.rs#648)    /// let bin_name = parser.bin_name().unwrap_or("myapp");
[649](https://docs.rs#649)    /// println!("{}: Some message", bin_name);
[650](https://docs.rs#650)    /// ```
[651](https://docs.rs#651)    pub fn bin_name(&self) -> Option<&str> {
[652](https://docs.rs#652)        Some(self.bin_name.as_ref()?)
[653](https://docs.rs#653)    }
[654](https://docs.rs#654)
[655](https://docs.rs#655)    /// Get a value only if it's concatenated to an option, as in `-ovalue` or
[656](https://docs.rs#656)    /// `--option=value` or `-o=value`, but not `-o value` or `--option value`.
[657](https://docs.rs#657)    pub fn optional_value(&mut self) -> Option<OsString> {
[658](https://docs.rs#658)        Some(self.raw_optional_value()?.0)
[659](https://docs.rs#659)    }
[660](https://docs.rs#660)
[661](https://docs.rs#661)    /// [`Parser::optional_value`], but indicate whether the value was joined
[662](https://docs.rs#662)    /// with an = sign. This matters for [`Parser::values`].
[663](https://docs.rs#663)    fn raw_optional_value(&mut self) -> Option<(OsString, bool)> {
[664](https://docs.rs#664)        match replace(&mut self.state, State::None) {
[665](https://docs.rs#665)            State::PendingValue(value) => Some((value, true)),
[666](https://docs.rs#666)            State::Shorts(mut arg, mut pos) => {
[667](https://docs.rs#667)                if pos >= arg.len() {
[668](https://docs.rs#668)                    return None;
[669](https://docs.rs#669)                }
[670](https://docs.rs#670)                let mut had_eq_sign = false;
[671](https://docs.rs#671)                if arg[pos] == b'=' && self.short_equals {
[672](https://docs.rs#672)                    // -o=value.
[673](https://docs.rs#673)                    // clap actually strips out all leading '='s, but that seems silly.
[674](https://docs.rs#674)                    // We allow `-xo=value`. Python's argparse doesn't strip the = in that case.
[675](https://docs.rs#675)                    pos += 1;
[676](https://docs.rs#676)                    had_eq_sign = true;
[677](https://docs.rs#677)                }
[678](https://docs.rs#678)                arg.drain(..pos); // Reuse allocation
[679](https://docs.rs#679)                #[cfg(unix)]
[680](https://docs.rs#680)                {
[681](https://docs.rs#681)                    Some((OsString::from_vec(arg), had_eq_sign))
[682](https://docs.rs#682)                }
[683](https://docs.rs#683)                #[cfg(not(unix))]
[684](https://docs.rs#684)                {
[685](https://docs.rs#685)                    let arg = String::from_utf8(arg)
[686](https://docs.rs#686)                        .expect("short option args on exotic platforms must be unicode");
[687](https://docs.rs#687)                    Some((arg.into(), had_eq_sign))
[688](https://docs.rs#688)                }
[689](https://docs.rs#689)            }
[690](https://docs.rs#690)            #[cfg(windows)]
[691](https://docs.rs#691)            State::ShortsU16(arg, mut pos) => {
[692](https://docs.rs#692)                if pos >= arg.len() {
[693](https://docs.rs#693)                    return None;
[694](https://docs.rs#694)                }
[695](https://docs.rs#695)                let mut had_eq_sign = false;
[696](https://docs.rs#696)                if arg[pos] == b'=' as u16 && self.short_equals {
[697](https://docs.rs#697)                    pos += 1;
[698](https://docs.rs#698)                    had_eq_sign = true;
[699](https://docs.rs#699)                }
[700](https://docs.rs#700)                Some((OsString::from_wide(&arg[pos..]), had_eq_sign))
[701](https://docs.rs#701)            }
[702](https://docs.rs#702)            State::FinishedOpts => {
[703](https://docs.rs#703)                // Not really supposed to be here, but it's benign and not our fault
[704](https://docs.rs#704)                self.state = State::FinishedOpts;
[705](https://docs.rs#705)                None
[706](https://docs.rs#706)            }
[707](https://docs.rs#707)            State::None => None,
[708](https://docs.rs#708)        }
[709](https://docs.rs#709)    }
[710](https://docs.rs#710)
[711](https://docs.rs#711)    fn new(bin_name: Option<OsString>, source: InnerIter) -> Parser {
[712](https://docs.rs#712)        Parser {
[713](https://docs.rs#713)            source,
[714](https://docs.rs#714)            state: State::None,
[715](https://docs.rs#715)            last_option: LastOption::None,
[716](https://docs.rs#716)            bin_name: bin_name.map(|s| match s.into_string() {
[717](https://docs.rs#717)                Ok(text) => text,
[718](https://docs.rs#718)                Err(text) => text.to_string_lossy().into_owned(),
[719](https://docs.rs#719)            }),
[720](https://docs.rs#720)            short_equals: true,
[721](https://docs.rs#721)        }
[722](https://docs.rs#722)    }

[724](https://docs.rs#724)    /// Create a parser from the environment using [`std::env::args_os`].
[725](https://docs.rs#725)    ///
[726](https://docs.rs#726)    /// This is the usual way to create a `Parser`.
[727](https://docs.rs#727)    pub fn from_env() -> Parser {
[728](https://docs.rs#728)        let mut source = make_iter(std::env::args_os());
[729](https://docs.rs#729)        Parser::new(source.next(), source)
[730](https://docs.rs#730)    }

[732](https://docs.rs#732)    // The collision with `FromIterator::from_iter` is a bit unfortunate.
[733](https://docs.rs#733)    // This name is used because:
[734](https://docs.rs#734)    // - `from_args()` was taken, and changing its behavior without changing
[735](https://docs.rs#735)    //   its signature would be evil.
[736](https://docs.rs#736)    // - structopt also had a method by that name, so there's a precedent.
[737](https://docs.rs#737)    //   (clap_derive doesn't.)
[738](https://docs.rs#738)    // - I couldn't think of a better one.
[739](https://docs.rs#739)    // When this name was chosen `FromIterator` could not actually be implemented.
[740](https://docs.rs#740)    // It can be implemented now, but I'm not sure there's a reason to.

[742](https://docs.rs#742)    /// Create a parser from an iterator. This is useful for testing among other things.
[743](https://docs.rs#743)    ///
[744](https://docs.rs#744)    /// The first item from the iterator **must** be the binary name, as from [`std::env::args_os`].
[745](https://docs.rs#745)    ///

[747](https://docs.rs#747)    ///

[749](https://docs.rs#749)    /// ```

[751](https://docs.rs#751)    /// ```
[752](https://docs.rs#752)    pub fn from_iter<I>(args: I) -> Parser
[753](https://docs.rs#753)    where
[754](https://docs.rs#754)        I: IntoIterator,

[756](https://docs.rs#756)    {
[757](https://docs.rs#757)        let mut args = make_iter(args.into_iter().map(Into::into));
[758](https://docs.rs#758)        Parser::new(args.next(), args)
[759](https://docs.rs#759)    }
[760](https://docs.rs#760)
[761](https://docs.rs#761)    /// Create a parser from an iterator that does **not** include the binary name.

[767](https://docs.rs#767)    pub fn from_args<I>(args: I) -> Parser

[773](https://docs.rs#773)    }

[775](https://docs.rs#775)    /// Store a long option so the caller can borrow it.
[776](https://docs.rs#776)    fn set_long(&mut self, option: String) -> Arg<'_> {

[778](https://docs.rs#778)        match self.last_option {
[779](https://docs.rs#779)            LastOption::Long(ref option) => Arg::Long(&option[2..]),
[780](https://docs.rs#780)            _ => unreachable!(),
