[783](https://docs.rs#783)
[784](https://docs.rs#784)    /// Configure whether to parse an equals sign (`=`) for short options.
[785](https://docs.rs#785)    ///
[786](https://docs.rs#786)    /// If this is **true** (the default), `-o=foobar` will be interpreted as
[787](https://docs.rs#787)    /// the option `-o` with the value `foobar`.
[788](https://docs.rs#788)    ///
[789](https://docs.rs#789)    /// If this is **false**, `-o=foobar` will be interpreted as
[790](https://docs.rs#790)    /// the option `-o` with the value `=foobar`.
[791](https://docs.rs#791)    ///
[792](https://docs.rs#792)    /// Note that even if this is `true` the equals sign is optional. That is,
[793](https://docs.rs#793)    /// `-ofoobar` and `-o foobar` are always interpreted as `-o` with the value
[794](https://docs.rs#794)    /// `foobar` regardless of this setting.
[795](https://docs.rs#795)    ///
[796](https://docs.rs#796)    /// Most other argument parsers treat the equals sign as part of the value,
[797](https://docs.rs#797)    /// but the syntax is notably accepted by [`clap`](https://docs.rs/clap/latest/clap/)
[798](https://docs.rs#798)    /// and by Python's [`argparse`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/argparse.html).
[799](https://docs.rs#799)    ///
[800](https://docs.rs#800)    /// You may want to disable this setting if it's common for an option's value
[801](https://docs.rs#801)    /// to start with an equals sign. The Unix `cut` command for example is sometimes
[802](https://docs.rs#802)    /// used with `-d=`, where `"="` is the value belonging to the `-d` option. By default
[803](https://docs.rs#803)    /// the empty string `""` is parsed instead.
[804](https://docs.rs#804)    ///
[805](https://docs.rs#805)    /// # Example
[806](https://docs.rs#806)    ///
[807](https://docs.rs#807)    /// You can configure this right after creating the parser:
[808](https://docs.rs#808)    /// ```
[809](https://docs.rs#809)    /// let mut parser = lexopt::Parser::from_env();
[810](https://docs.rs#810)    /// parser.set_short_equals(false);
[811](https://docs.rs#811)    /// ```
[812](https://docs.rs#812)    ///
[813](https://docs.rs#813)    /// You could also do it temporarily, for an individual option:
[814](https://docs.rs#814)    /// ```
[815](https://docs.rs#815)    /// # fn main() -> Result<(), lexopt::Error> {
[816](https://docs.rs#816)    /// # use lexopt::prelude::*;
[817](https://docs.rs#817)    /// # let mut parser = lexopt::Parser::from_args(&["-d=", "key=value"]);
[818](https://docs.rs#818)    /// # let mut delimiter = None;
[819](https://docs.rs#819)    /// # while let Some(arg) = parser.next()? {
[820](https://docs.rs#820)    /// # match arg {
[821](https://docs.rs#821)    /// Short('d') | Long("delimiter") => {
[822](https://docs.rs#822)    ///     parser.set_short_equals(false);
[823](https://docs.rs#823)    ///     delimiter = Some(parser.value()?.string()?);
[824](https://docs.rs#824)    ///     parser.set_short_equals(true);
[825](https://docs.rs#825)    /// }
[826](https://docs.rs#826)    /// # _ => (), }} Ok(()) }
[827](https://docs.rs#827)    /// ```
[828](https://docs.rs#828)    pub fn set_short_equals(&mut self, on: bool) {
[829](https://docs.rs#829)        self.short_equals = on;
[830](https://docs.rs#830)    }
[831](https://docs.rs#831)}
[832](https://docs.rs#832)

[837](https://docs.rs#837)            Arg::Short(short) => Error::UnexpectedOption(format!("-{}", short)),
[838](https://docs.rs#838)            Arg::Long(long) => Error::UnexpectedOption(format!("--{}", long)),
[839](https://docs.rs#839)            Arg::Value(value) => Error::UnexpectedArgument(value),
[840](https://docs.rs#840)        }
[841](https://docs.rs#841)    }

[844](https://docs.rs#844)/// An iterator for multiple option-arguments, returned by [`Parser::values`].
[845](https://docs.rs#845)///
[846](https://docs.rs#846)/// It's guaranteed to yield at least one value.
[847](https://docs.rs#847)#[derive(Debug)]
[848](https://docs.rs#848)pub struct ValuesIter<'a> {
[849](https://docs.rs#849)    took_first: bool,
[850](https://docs.rs#850)    parser: Option<&'a mut Parser>,
[851](https://docs.rs#851)}
[852](https://docs.rs#852)
[853](https://docs.rs#853)impl Iterator for ValuesIter<'_> {
[854](https://docs.rs#854)    type Item = OsString;
[855](https://docs.rs#855)
[856](https://docs.rs#856)    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item> {
[857](https://docs.rs#857)        let parser = self.parser.as_mut()?;
[858](https://docs.rs#858)        if self.took_first {
[859](https://docs.rs#859)            parser.next_if_normal()
[860](https://docs.rs#860)        } else if let Some((value, had_eq_sign)) = parser.raw_optional_value() {
[861](https://docs.rs#861)            if had_eq_sign {
[862](https://docs.rs#862)                self.parser = None;
[863](https://docs.rs#863)            }
[864](https://docs.rs#864)            self.took_first = true;
[865](https://docs.rs#865)            Some(value)
[866](https://docs.rs#866)        } else {
[867](https://docs.rs#867)            let value = parser
[868](https://docs.rs#868)                .next_if_normal()
[869](https://docs.rs#869)                .expect("ValuesIter must yield at least one value");
[870](https://docs.rs#870)            self.took_first = true;
[871](https://docs.rs#871)            Some(value)
[872](https://docs.rs#872)        }
[873](https://docs.rs#873)    }
[874](https://docs.rs#874)}

[899](https://docs.rs#899)    /// Consume and return the next argument if a condition is true.
[900](https://docs.rs#900)    ///

[902](https://docs.rs#902)    pub fn next_if(&mut self, func: impl FnOnce(&OsStr) -> bool) -> Option<OsString> {
[903](https://docs.rs#903)        match self.peek() {
[904](https://docs.rs#904)            Some(arg) if func(arg) => self.next(),
[905](https://docs.rs#905)            _ => None,
[906](https://docs.rs#906)        }
[907](https://docs.rs#907)    }

[924](https://docs.rs#924)
[925](https://docs.rs#925)/// An error during argument parsing.
[926](https://docs.rs#926)///
[927](https://docs.rs#927)/// This implements `From<String>` and `From<&str>`, for easy ad-hoc error
[928](https://docs.rs#928)/// messages.
[929](https://docs.rs#929)//
[930](https://docs.rs#930)// This is not #[non_exhaustive] because of the MSRV. I'm hoping no more
[931](https://docs.rs#931)// variants will turn out to be needed: this seems reasonable, if the scope
[932](https://docs.rs#932)// of the library doesn't change. Worst case scenario it can be stuffed inside
[933](https://docs.rs#933)// Error::Custom.
[934](https://docs.rs#934)pub enum Error {
[935](https://docs.rs#935)    /// An option argument was expected but was not found.
[936](https://docs.rs#936)    MissingValue {
[937](https://docs.rs#937)        /// The most recently emitted option.
[938](https://docs.rs#938)        option: Option<String>,
[939](https://docs.rs#939)    },
[940](https://docs.rs#940)
[941](https://docs.rs#941)    /// An unexpected option was found.
[942](https://docs.rs#942)    UnexpectedOption(String),

[972](https://docs.rs#972)impl Display for Error {
[973](https://docs.rs#973)    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut std::fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> std::fmt::Result {
[974](https://docs.rs#974)        use crate::Error::*;
[975](https://docs.rs#975)        match self {
[976](https://docs.rs#976)            MissingValue { option: None } => write!(f, "missing argument"),
[977](https://docs.rs#977)            MissingValue {
[978](https://docs.rs#978)                option: Some(option),
[979](https://docs.rs#979)            } => {
[980](https://docs.rs#980)                write!(f, "missing argument for option '{}'", option)
[981](https://docs.rs#981)            }
[982](https://docs.rs#982)            UnexpectedOption(option) => write!(f, "invalid option '{}'", option),
[983](https://docs.rs#983)            UnexpectedArgument(value) => write!(f, "unexpected argument {:?}", value),
[984](https://docs.rs#984)            UnexpectedValue { option, value } => {
[985](https://docs.rs#985)                write!(
[986](https://docs.rs#986)                    f,
[987](https://docs.rs#987)                    "unexpected argument for option '{}': {:?}",
[988](https://docs.rs#988)                    option, value
[989](https://docs.rs#989)                )
[990](https://docs.rs#990)            }
[991](https://docs.rs#991)            NonUnicodeValue(value) => write!(f, "argument is invalid unicode: {:?}", value),
[992](https://docs.rs#992)            ParsingFailed { value, error } => {
[993](https://docs.rs#993)                write!(f, "cannot parse argument {:?}: {}", value, error)
[994](https://docs.rs#994)            }
[995](https://docs.rs#995)            Custom(err) => write!(f, "{}", err),
[996](https://docs.rs#996)        }
[997](https://docs.rs#997)    }

[1043](https://docs.rs#1043)/// An optional extension trait with methods for parsing [`OsString`]s.
[1044](https://docs.rs#1044)///
[1045](https://docs.rs#1045)/// They may fail in two cases:
[1046](https://docs.rs#1046)/// - The value cannot be decoded because it's invalid unicode
[1047](https://docs.rs#1047)///   ([`Error::NonUnicodeValue`])
[1048](https://docs.rs#1048)/// - The value can be decoded, but parsing fails ([`Error::ParsingFailed`])
[1049](https://docs.rs#1049)///
[1050](https://docs.rs#1050)/// If parsing fails the error will be wrapped in lexopt's own [`Error`] type.
[1051](https://docs.rs#1051)pub trait ValueExt: private::Sealed {
[1052](https://docs.rs#1052)    /// Decode the value and parse it using [`FromStr`].
[1053](https://docs.rs#1053)    ///
[1054](https://docs.rs#1054)    /// This will fail if the value is not valid unicode or if the subsequent
[1055](https://docs.rs#1055)    /// parsing fails.
[1056](https://docs.rs#1056)    fn parse<T: FromStr>(&self) -> Result<T, Error>
[1057](https://docs.rs#1057)    where
[1058](https://docs.rs#1058)        T::Err: Into<Box<dyn std::error::Error + Send + Sync + 'static>>;
[1059](https://docs.rs#1059)
[1060](https://docs.rs#1060)    // TODO: move the F parameter to the end for better turbofishing.
[1061](https://docs.rs#1061)    // This is a breaking change that affects at least one real-world program.
[1062](https://docs.rs#1062)    // But the code will be better off for it, so it's worth doing in the next
[1063](https://docs.rs#1063)    // breaking release.
[1064](https://docs.rs#1064)
[1065](https://docs.rs#1065)    /// Decode the value and parse it using a custom function.
[1066](https://docs.rs#1066)    fn parse_with<F, T, E>(&self, func: F) -> Result<T, Error>
[1067](https://docs.rs#1067)    where
[1068](https://docs.rs#1068)        F: FnOnce(&str) -> Result<T, E>,
[1069](https://docs.rs#1069)        E: Into<Box<dyn std::error::Error + Send + Sync + 'static>>;
[1070](https://docs.rs#1070)
[1071](https://docs.rs#1071)    // There is no parse_os_with() because I can't think of any useful
[1072](https://docs.rs#1072)    // fallible operations on an OsString. Typically you'd either decode it,
[1073](https://docs.rs#1073)    // use it as is, or do an infallible conversion to a PathBuf or such.
[1074](https://docs.rs#1074)    //
[1075](https://docs.rs#1075)    // If you have a use for parse_os_with() please open an issue with an
[1076](https://docs.rs#1076)    // example.
[1077](https://docs.rs#1077)
[1078](https://docs.rs#1078)    /// Convert the `OsString` into a [`String`] if it's valid Unicode.
[1079](https://docs.rs#1079)    ///
[1080](https://docs.rs#1080)    /// This is like [`OsString::into_string`] but returns an
[1081](https://docs.rs#1081)    /// [`Error::NonUnicodeValue`] on error instead of the original `OsString`.
[1082](https://docs.rs#1082)    /// This makes it easier to propagate the failure with libraries like
[1083](https://docs.rs#1083)    /// `anyhow`.
[1084](https://docs.rs#1084)    fn string(self) -> Result<String, Error>;
[1085](https://docs.rs#1085)}
[1086](https://docs.rs#1086)
[1087](https://docs.rs#1087)impl ValueExt for OsString {
[1088](https://docs.rs#1088)    fn parse<T: FromStr>(&self) -> Result<T, Error>
[1089](https://docs.rs#1089)    where
[1090](https://docs.rs#1090)        T::Err: Into<Box<dyn std::error::Error + Send + Sync + 'static>>,
[1091](https://docs.rs#1091)    {
[1092](https://docs.rs#1092)        self.parse_with(FromStr::from_str)
[1093](https://docs.rs#1093)    }
[1094](https://docs.rs#1094)
[1095](https://docs.rs#1095)    fn parse_with<F, T, E>(&self, func: F) -> Result<T, Error>
[1096](https://docs.rs#1096)    where
[1097](https://docs.rs#1097)        F: FnOnce(&str) -> Result<T, E>,
[1098](https://docs.rs#1098)        E: Into<Box<dyn std::error::Error + Send + Sync + 'static>>,
[1099](https://docs.rs#1099)    {
[1100](https://docs.rs#1100)        match self.to_str() {
[1101](https://docs.rs#1101)            Some(text) => match func(text) {
[1102](https://docs.rs#1102)                Ok(value) => Ok(value),
[1103](https://docs.rs#1103)                Err(err) => Err(Error::ParsingFailed {
[1104](https://docs.rs#1104)                    value: text.to_owned(),
[1105](https://docs.rs#1105)                    error: err.into(),
[1106](https://docs.rs#1106)                }),
[1107](https://docs.rs#1107)            },
[1108](https://docs.rs#1108)            None => Err(Error::NonUnicodeValue(self.into())),
[1109](https://docs.rs#1109)        }
[1110](https://docs.rs#1110)    }
[1111](https://docs.rs#1111)
[1112](https://docs.rs#1112)    fn string(self) -> Result<String, Error> {
[1113](https://docs.rs#1113)        match self.into_string() {
[1114](https://docs.rs#1114)            Ok(string) => Ok(string),
[1115](https://docs.rs#1115)            Err(raw) => Err(Error::NonUnicodeValue(raw)),
[1116](https://docs.rs#1116)        }
[1117](https://docs.rs#1117)    }

[1120](https://docs.rs#1120)/// A small prelude for processing arguments.
[1121](https://docs.rs#1121)///
[1122](https://docs.rs#1122)/// It allows you to write `Short`/`Long`/`Value` without an [`Arg`] prefix
[1123](https://docs.rs#1123)/// and adds convenience methods to [`OsString`].
[1124](https://docs.rs#1124)///
[1125](https://docs.rs#1125)/// If this is used it's best to import it inside a function, not in module
[1126](https://docs.rs#1126)/// scope:
[1127](https://docs.rs#1127)/// ```
[1128](https://docs.rs#1128)/// # struct Args;
[1129](https://docs.rs#1129)/// fn parse_args() -> Result<Args, lexopt::Error> {
[1130](https://docs.rs#1130)///     use lexopt::prelude::*;
[1131](https://docs.rs#1131)///     // ...
[1132](https://docs.rs#1132)///     # Ok(Args)
[1133](https://docs.rs#1133)/// }
[1134](https://docs.rs#1134)/// ```
[1135](https://docs.rs#1135)pub mod prelude {
[1136](https://docs.rs#1136)    pub use super::Arg::*;
[1137](https://docs.rs#1137)    pub use super::ValueExt;
[1138](https://docs.rs#1138)}

[1140](https://docs.rs#1140)/// Take the first codepoint from a UTF-8 bytestring.
[1141](https://docs.rs#1141)///
[1142](https://docs.rs#1142)/// The rest of the bytestring does not have to be valid unicode.
[1143](https://docs.rs#1143)fn first_codepoint(bytes: &[u8]) -> Result<Option<char>, Utf8Error> {
[1144](https://docs.rs#1144)    // We only need the first 4 bytes
[1145](https://docs.rs#1145)    let bytes = bytes.get(..4).unwrap_or(bytes);
[1146](https://docs.rs#1146)    let text = match std::str::from_utf8(bytes) {
[1147](https://docs.rs#1147)        Ok(text) => text,
[1148](https://docs.rs#1148)        Err(err) if err.valid_up_to() > 0 => {
[1149](https://docs.rs#1149)            std::str::from_utf8(&bytes[..err.valid_up_to()]).unwrap()
[1150](https://docs.rs#1150)        }
[1151](https://docs.rs#1151)        Err(err) => return Err(err),
[1152](https://docs.rs#1152)    };
[1153](https://docs.rs#1153)    Ok(text.chars().next())
[1154](https://docs.rs#1154)}
[1155](https://docs.rs#1155)
[1156](https://docs.rs#1156)#[cfg(windows)]
[1157](https://docs.rs#1157)/// As before, but for UTF-16.
[1158](https://docs.rs#1158)fn first_utf16_codepoint(units: &[u16]) -> Result<Option<char>, u16> {
[1159](https://docs.rs#1159)    match std::char::decode_utf16(units.iter().cloned()).next() {
[1160](https://docs.rs#1160)        Some(Ok(ch)) => Ok(Some(ch)),
[1161](https://docs.rs#1161)        Some(Err(_)) => Err(units[0]),
[1162](https://docs.rs#1162)        None => Ok(None),
[1163](https://docs.rs#1163)    }

[1889](https://docs.rs#1889)    /// Transform @ characters into invalid unicode.
[1890](https://docs.rs#1890)    fn bad_string(text: &str) -> OsString {
[1891](https://docs.rs#1891)        #[cfg(any(unix, all(target_os = "wasi", target_env = "p1")))]
[1892](https://docs.rs#1892)        {
[1893](https://docs.rs#1893)            let mut text = text.as_bytes().to_vec();
[1894](https://docs.rs#1894)            for ch in &mut text {
[1895](https://docs.rs#1895)                if *ch == b'@' {
[1896](https://docs.rs#1896)                    *ch = b'\xFF';
[1897](https://docs.rs#1897)                }
[1898](https://docs.rs#1898)            }
[1899](https://docs.rs#1899)            OsString::from_vec(text)
[1900](https://docs.rs#1900)        }
[1901](https://docs.rs#1901)        #[cfg(windows)]
[1902](https://docs.rs#1902)        {
[1903](https://docs.rs#1903)            let mut out = Vec::new();
[1904](https://docs.rs#1904)            for ch in text.chars() {
[1905](https://docs.rs#1905)                if ch == '@' {
[1906](https://docs.rs#1906)                    out.push(0xD800);
[1907](https://docs.rs#1907)                } else {
[1908](https://docs.rs#1908)                    let mut buf = [0; 2];
[1909](https://docs.rs#1909)                    out.extend(&*ch.encode_utf16(&mut buf));
[1910](https://docs.rs#1910)                }
[1911](https://docs.rs#1911)            }
[1912](https://docs.rs#1912)            OsString::from_wide(&out)
[1913](https://docs.rs#1913)        }
[1914](https://docs.rs#1914)        #[cfg(not(any(unix, windows, all(target_os = "wasi", target_env = "p1"))))]
[1915](https://docs.rs#1915)        {
[1916](https://docs.rs#1916)            if text.contains('@') {
[1917](https://docs.rs#1917)                unimplemented!("Don't know how to create invalid OsStrings on this platform");
[1918](https://docs.rs#1918)            }

# Parser in lexopt - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/lexopt/0.3.2/lexopt/struct.Parser.html

`pub struct Parser { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A parser for command line arguments.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Get the next option or positional argument.

A return value of `Ok(None)` means the command line has been exhausted.

Options that are not valid unicode are transformed with replacement
characters as by [ String::from_utf8_lossy](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html#method.from_utf8_lossy).

[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

[ Error::UnexpectedValue](https://docs.rs/enum.Error.html#variant.UnexpectedValue) is returned if the last option had a
value that hasn’t been consumed, as in

`--option=value` or `-o=value`.It’s possible to continue parsing after an error (but this is rarely useful).

```
17fn main() -> Result<(), lexopt::Error> {
18    use lexopt::prelude::*;
19
20    let mut parser = lexopt::Parser::from_env();
21    parser.set_short_equals(false);
22    let mut free = Vec::new();
23    while let Some(arg) = parser.next()? {
24        match arg {
25            Short('n') | Long("number") => {
26                let num: u16 = parser.value()?.parse()?;
27                println!("Got number {}", num);
28            }
29            Long("shout") => {
30                println!("Got --shout");
31            }
32            Value(val) => {
33                free.push(val);
34                free.extend(parser.raw_args()?);
35            }
36            _ => return Err(arg.unexpected()),
37        }
38    }
39    println!("Got free args {:?}", free);
40    Ok(())
41}
```

49fn parse_args() -> Result<AppArgs, lexopt::Error> {

```
9fn main() -> Result<(), lexopt::Error> {
10    use lexopt::prelude::*;
11
12    let mut settings = GlobalSettings {
13        toolchain: "stable".to_owned(),
14        color: Color::Auto,
15        offline: false,
16        quiet: false,
17        verbose: false,
18    };
19
20    let mut parser = lexopt::Parser::from_env();
21    while let Some(arg) = parser.next()? {
22        match arg {
23            Long("color") => {
24                settings.color = parser.value()?.parse()?;
25            }
26            Long("offline") => {
27                settings.offline = true;
28            }
29            Long("quiet") => {
30                settings.quiet = true;
31                settings.verbose = false;
32            }
33            Long("verbose") => {
34                settings.verbose = true;
35                settings.quiet = false;
36            }
37            Long("help") => {
38                println!("{}", HELP);
39                std::process::exit(0);
40            }
41            Value(value) => {
42                let value = value.string()?;
43                match value.as_str() {
44                    value if value.starts_with('+') => {
45                        settings.toolchain = value[1..].to_owned();
46                    }
47                    "install" => {
48                        return install(settings, parser);
49                    }
50                    value => {
51                        return Err(format!("unknown subcommand '{}'", value).into());
52                    }
53                }
54            }
55            _ => return Err(arg.unexpected()),
56        }
57    }
58
59    println!("{}", HELP);
60    Ok(())
61}
62
63#[derive(Debug)]
64struct GlobalSettings {
65    toolchain: String,
66    color: Color,
67    offline: bool,
68    quiet: bool,
69    verbose: bool,
70}
71
72fn install(settings: GlobalSettings, mut parser: lexopt::Parser) -> Result<(), lexopt::Error> {
73    use lexopt::prelude::*;
74
75    let mut package: Option<String> = None;
76    let mut root: Option<PathBuf> = None;
77    let mut jobs: u16 = get_no_of_cpus();
78
79    while let Some(arg) = parser.next()? {
80        match arg {
81            Value(value) if package.is_none() => {
82                package = Some(value.string()?);
83            }
84            Long("root") => {
85                root = Some(parser.value()?.into());
86            }
87            Short('j') | Long("jobs") => {
88                jobs = parser.value()?.parse()?;
89            }
90            Long("help") => {
91                println!("cargo install [OPTIONS] CRATE");
92                std::process::exit(0);
93            }
94            _ => return Err(arg.unexpected()),
95        }
96    }
97
98    println!("Settings: {:#?}", settings);
99    println!(
100        "Installing {} into {:?} with {} jobs",
101        package.ok_or("missing CRATE argument")?,
102        root,
103        jobs
104    );
105
106    Ok(())
107}
```
Get a value for an option.

This function should normally be called right after seeing an option
that expects a value, with positional arguments being collected
using [ next()](https://docs.rs/struct.Parser.html#method.next).

A value is collected even if it looks like an option
(i.e., starts with `-`).

[§](https://docs.rs#errors-1)Errors

An [ Error::MissingValue](https://docs.rs/enum.Error.html#variant.MissingValue) is returned if the end of the command
line is reached.

```

86            }
87            Short('j') | Long("jobs") => {
88                jobs = parser.value()?.parse()?;
89            }
90            Long("help") => {
91                println!("cargo install [OPTIONS] CRATE");
92                std::process::exit(0);
93            }
94            _ => return Err(arg.unexpected()),
95        }
96    }
97
98    println!("Settings: {:#?}", settings);
99    println!(
100        "Installing {} into {:?} with {} jobs",
101        package.ok_or("missing CRATE argument")?,
102        root,
103        jobs
104    );
105
106    Ok(())
107}
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/lexopt/lib.rs.html#459-475)#### pub fn [values](https://docs.rs#method.values)(&mut self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[ValuesIter](https://docs.rs/struct.ValuesIter.html)<'_>, [Error](https://docs.rs/enum.Error.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/lexopt/lib.rs.html#459-475)

#### pub fn [values](https://docs.rs#method.values)(&mut self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[ValuesIter](https://docs.rs/struct.ValuesIter.html)<'_>, [Error](https://docs.rs/enum.Error.html)>

Gather multiple values for an option.

This is used for options that take multiple arguments, such as a
`--command` flag that’s invoked as `app --command echo 'Hello world'`.

It will gather arguments until another option is found, or `--` is found, or
the end of the command line is reached. This differs from `.value()`, which
takes a value even if it looks like an option.

On success the resulting iterator will yield at least one value.

An equals sign (`=`) will limit this to a single value. That means `-a=b c` and
`--opt=b c` will only yield `"b"` while `-a b c`, `-ab c` and `--opt b c` will
yield `"b"`, `"c"`.

(If [ short_equals](https://docs.rs/struct.Parser.html#method.set_short_equals) is disabled then

`-a=b c` will yield
`"=b"`, `"c"`.)[§](https://docs.rs#errors-2)Errors

If not at least one value is found then [ Error::MissingValue](https://docs.rs/enum.Error.html#variant.MissingValue) is returned.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
let arguments: Vec<OsString> = parser.values()?.collect();
let at_most_three_files: Vec<PathBuf> = parser.values()?.take(3).map(Into::into).collect();
for value in parser.values()? {
    // ...
}
```
Take raw arguments from the original command line.

This returns an iterator of [ OsString](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/ffi/os_str/struct.OsString.html)s. Any arguments that are not
consumed are kept, so you can continue parsing after you’re done with
the iterator.

To inspect an argument without consuming it, use [ RawArgs::peek](https://docs.rs/struct.RawArgs.html#method.peek) or

[.](https://docs.rs/struct.RawArgs.html#method.as_slice)

`RawArgs::as_slice`[§](https://docs.rs#errors-3)Errors

Returns an [ Error::UnexpectedValue](https://docs.rs/enum.Error.html#variant.UnexpectedValue) if the last option had a left-over
argument, as in

`--option=value`, `-ovalue`, or if it was midway through
an option chain, as in `-abc`. The iterator only yields whole arguments.
To avoid this, use [.](https://docs.rs/struct.Parser.html#method.try_raw_args)

`try_raw_args()`After this error the method is guaranteed to succeed, as it consumes the rest of the argument.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-1)Example

As soon as a free-standing argument is found, consume the other arguments as-is, and build them into a command.

```
Value(prog) => {
    let args: Vec<_> = parser.raw_args()?.collect();
    let command = std::process::Command::new(prog).args(args);
}
```
```
17fn main() -> Result<(), lexopt::Error> {

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/lexopt/lib.rs.html#608-614)#### pub fn [try_raw_args](https://docs.rs#method.try_raw_args)(&mut self) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[RawArgs](https://docs.rs/struct.RawArgs.html)<'_>>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/lexopt/lib.rs.html#608-614)

#### pub fn [try_raw_args](https://docs.rs#method.try_raw_args)(&mut self) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[RawArgs](https://docs.rs/struct.RawArgs.html)<'_>>

Take raw arguments from the original command line, *if* the current argument
has finished processing.

Unlike [ raw_args()](https://docs.rs/struct.Parser.html#method.raw_args) this does not consume any value
in case of a left-over argument. This makes it safe to call at any time.

It returns `None` exactly when [ optional_value()](https://docs.rs/struct.Parser.html#method.optional_value)
would return

`Some`.Note: If no arguments are left then it returns an empty iterator (not `None`).

[§](https://docs.rs#example-2)Example

Process arguments of the form `-123` as numbers. For a complete runnable version of
this example, see
[ examples/nonstandard.rs](https://github.com/blyxxyz/lexopt/blob/e3754e6f24506afb42394602fc257b1ad9258d84/examples/nonstandard.rs).

```
fn parse_dashnum(parser: &mut lexopt::Parser) -> Option<u64> {
    let mut raw = parser.try_raw_args()?;
    let arg = raw.peek()?.to_str()?;
    let num = arg.strip_prefix('-')?.parse::<u64>().ok()?;
    raw.next(); // Consume the argument we just parsed
    Some(num)
}
loop {
    if let Some(num) = parse_dashnum(&mut parser) {
        println!("Got number {}", num);
    } else if let Some(arg) = parser.next()? {
        match arg {
            // ...
        }
    } else {
        break;
    }
}
```

Create a parser from an iterator. This is useful for testing among other things.

The first item from the iterator **must** be the binary name, as from [ std::env::args_os](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/env/fn.args_os.html).

The iterator is consumed immediately.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-4)Example

`let mut parser = lexopt::Parser::from_iter(&["myapp", "-n", "10", "./foo.bar"]);`[Source](https://docs.rs/src/lexopt/lib.rs.html#828-830)#### pub fn [set_short_equals](https://docs.rs#method.set_short_equals)(&mut self, on: [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html))

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/lexopt/lib.rs.html#828-830)

#### pub fn [set_short_equals](https://docs.rs#method.set_short_equals)(&mut self, on: [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html))

Configure whether to parse an equals sign (`=`) for short options.

If this is **true** (the default), `-o=foobar` will be interpreted as
the option `-o` with the value `foobar`.

If this is **false**, `-o=foobar` will be interpreted as
the option `-o` with the value `=foobar`.

Note that even if this is `true` the equals sign is optional. That is,
`-ofoobar` and `-o foobar` are always interpreted as `-o` with the value
`foobar` regardless of this setting.

Most other argument parsers treat the equals sign as part of the value,
but the syntax is notably accepted by [ clap](https://docs.rs/clap/latest/clap/)
and by Python’s

[.](https://docs.python.org/3/library/argparse.html)

`argparse`You may want to disable this setting if it’s common for an option’s value
to start with an equals sign. The Unix `cut` command for example is sometimes
used with `-d=`, where `"="` is the value belonging to the `-d` option. By default
the empty string `""` is parsed instead.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-5)Example

You can configure this right after creating the parser:

```
let mut parser = lexopt::Parser::from_env();
parser.set_short_equals(false);
```
You could also do it temporarily, for an individual option:

```
Short('d') | Long("delimiter") => {
    parser.set_short_equals(false);
    delimiter = Some(parser.value()?.string()?);
    parser.set_short_equals(true);
}
```
```

## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Short)

### Short([char](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html))

A short option, e.g. `Short('q')` for `-q`.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Long)

### Long(&'a [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html))

A long option, e.g. `Long("verbose")` for `--verbose`. (The dashes are not included.)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Value)

### Value([OsString](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/ffi/os_str/struct.OsString.html))

A positional argument, e.g. `/dev/null`.

72fn install(settings: GlobalSettings, mut parser: lexopt::Parser) -> Result<(), lexopt::Error> {
73    use lexopt::prelude::*;
74
75    let mut package: Option<String> = None;
76    let mut root: Option<PathBuf> = None;
77    let mut jobs: u16 = get_no_of_cpus();
78
79    while let Some(arg) = parser.next()? {
80        match arg {
81            Value(value) if package.is_none() => {
82                package = Some(value.string()?);
83            }
84            Long("root") => {
85                root = Some(parser.value()?.into());
86            }
87            Short('j') | Long("jobs") => {
88                jobs = parser.value()?.parse()?;
89            }
90            Long("help") => {
91                println!("cargo install [OPTIONS] CRATE");
92                std::process::exit(0);
93            }
94            _ => return Err(arg.unexpected()),
95        }
96    }
97
98    println!("Settings: {:#?}", settings);
99    println!(
100        "Installing {} into {:?} with {} jobs",
101        package.ok_or("missing CRATE argument")?,
102        root,
103        jobs
104    );
105
106    Ok(())
107}
```

# lexopt::prelude - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/lexopt/0.3.2/lexopt/prelude/index.html

## Expand description

A small prelude for processing arguments.

It allows you to write `Short`/`Long`/`Value` without an [ Arg](https://docs.rs/enum.Arg.html) prefix
and adds convenience methods to

[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/ffi/os_str/struct.OsString.html)

`OsString`If this is used it’s best to import it inside a function, not in module scope:

```
fn parse_args() -> Result<Args, lexopt::Error> {
    use lexopt::prelude::*;
    // ...
}
```

}## Expand description

An optional extension trait with methods for parsing [ OsString](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/ffi/os_str/struct.OsString.html)s.

They may fail in two cases:

- The value cannot be decoded because it’s invalid unicode
(`Error::NonUnicodeValue`
- The value can be decoded, but parsing fails (`Error::ParsingFailed`

If parsing fails the error will be wrapped in lexopt’s own [ Error](https://docs.rs/enum.Error.html) type.

Decode the value and parse it using a custom function.

Convert the `OsString` into a [ String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html) if it’s valid Unicode.

This is like [ OsString::into_string](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/ffi/os_str/struct.OsString.html#method.into_string) but returns an

[on error instead of the original](https://docs.rs/enum.Error.html#variant.NonUnicodeValue)

`Error::NonUnicodeValue``OsString`.
This makes it easier to propagate the failure with libraries like
`anyhow`.## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

# lexopt - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/lexopt/latest/lexopt/

## Expand description

A pathologically simple command line argument parser.

Most argument parsers are declarative: you tell them what to parse, and they do it.

This one provides you with a stream of options and values and lets you figure out the rest.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
struct Args {
    thing: String,
    number: u32,
    shout: bool,
}
fn parse_args() -> Result<Args, lexopt::Error> {
    use lexopt::prelude::*;
    let mut thing = None;
    let mut number = 1;
    let mut shout = false;
    let mut parser = lexopt::Parser::from_env();
    while let Some(arg) = parser.next()? {
        match arg {
            Short('n') | Long("number") => {
                number = parser.value()?.parse()?;
            }
            Long("shout") => {
                shout = true;
            }
            Value(val) if thing.is_none() => {
                thing = Some(val.string()?);
            }
            Long("help") => {
                println!("Usage: hello [-n|--number=NUM] [--shout] THING");
                std::process::exit(0);
            }
            _ => return Err(arg.unexpected()),
        }
    }
    Ok(Args {
        thing: thing.ok_or("missing argument THING")?,
        number,
        shout,
    })
}
fn main() -> Result<(), lexopt::Error> {
    let args = parse_args()?;
    let mut message = format!("Hello {}", args.thing);
    if args.shout {
        message = message.to_uppercase();
    }
    for _ in 0..args.number {
        println!("{}", message);
    }
    Ok(())
}
```
Let’s walk through this:

- We start parsing with `Parser::from_env`
- We call `parser.next()`
- We match on arguments. `Short``Long`
- To get the value that belongs to an option (like `10`in`-n 10`) we call`parser.value()`- This returns a standard `OsString`
- For convenience, `use lexopt::prelude::*``.parse()``str::parse`
- Calling `parser.value()`is how we tell`Parser`that`-n`takes a value at all.

- This returns a standard
- `Value`indicates a free-standing argument.- `if thing.is_none()`is a useful pattern for positional arguments. If we already found- `thing`we pass it on to another case.
- It also contains an `OsString`.- The `.string()``String`.

- The

- If we don’t know what to do with an argument we use `return Err(arg.unexpected())`
- Strings can be promoted to errors for custom error messages.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)
- A small prelude for processing arguments.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Parser](https://docs.rs/struct.Parser.html)
- A parser for command line arguments.
- [RawArgs](https://docs.rs/struct.RawArgs.html)
- An iterator for the remaining raw arguments, returned by `Parser::raw_args`
- [Values](https://docs.rs/struct.ValuesIter.html)- Iter
- An iterator for multiple option-arguments, returned by `Parser::values`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

# lexopt 0.3.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/lexopt/0.3.1

# Lexopt

Lexopt is an argument parser for Rust. It tries to have the simplest possible design that's still correct. It's so simple that it's a bit tedious to use.

Lexopt is:

- Small: one file, no dependencies, no macros. Easy to audit or vendor.
- Correct: standard conventions are supported and ambiguity is avoided. Tested and fuzzed.
- Pedantic: arguments are returned as `OsString`
- Imperative: options are returned as they are found, nothing is declared ahead of time.
- Minimalist: only basic functionality is provided.
- Unhelpful: there is no help generation and error messages often lack context.

## Example

```
```
Let's walk through this:

- We start parsing with `Parser::from_env()`.
- We call `parser.next()`in a loop to get all the arguments until they run out.
- We match on arguments. `Short`and`Long`indicate an option.
- To get the value that belongs to an option (like `10`in`-n 10`) we call`parser.value()`.- This returns a standard `OsString`- For convenience, `use lexopt::prelude::*`adds a`.parse()`method, analogous to[the one on](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.str.html#method.parse).`&str`

- For convenience,
- Calling `parser.value()`is how we tell`Parser`that`-n`takes a value at all.

- This returns a standard
- `Value`indicates a free-standing argument.- `if thing.is_none()`is a useful pattern for positional arguments. If we already found- `thing`we pass it on to another case.
- It also contains an `OsString`.- The `.string()`method decodes it into a plain`String`.

- The

- If we don't know what to do with an argument we use `return Err(arg.unexpected())`to turn it into an error message.
- Strings can be promoted to errors for custom error messages.

This covers most of the functionality in the library. Lexopt does very little for you.

For a larger example with useful patterns, see [ examples/cargo.rs](https://docs.rs/examples/cargo.rs).

## Command line syntax

The following conventions are supported:

- Short options (`-q`)
- Long options (`--verbose`)
- `--`to mark the end of options
- `=`to separate options from values (- `--option=value`,- `-o=value`)
- Spaces to separate options from values (`--option value`,`-o value`)
- Unseparated short options (`-ovalue`)
- Combined short options (`-abc`to mean`-a -b -c`)
- Options with optional arguments (like GNU sed's `-i`, which can be used standalone or as`-iSUFFIX`) (`Parser::optional_value()`
- Options with multiple arguments (`Parser::values()`

These are not supported out of the box:

- Single-dash long options (like find's `-name`)
- Abbreviated long options (GNU's getopt lets you write `--num`instead of`--number`if it can be expanded unambiguously)

[ Parser::raw_args()](https://docs.rs/lexopt/latest/lexopt/struct.Parser.html#method.raw_args) and

[provide an escape hatch for consuming the original command line. This can be used for custom syntax, like treating](https://docs.rs/lexopt/latest/lexopt/struct.Parser.html#method.try_raw_args)

`Parser::try_raw_args()``-123` as a number instead of a string of options. See [for an example of this.](https://docs.rs/examples/nonstandard.rs)

`examples/nonstandard.rs`## Unicode

This library supports unicode while tolerating non-unicode arguments.

Short options may be unicode, but only a single codepoint (a `char`).

Options can be combined with non-unicode arguments. That is, `--option=���` will not cause an error or mangle the value.

Options themselves are patched as by [ String::from_utf8_lossy](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/string/struct.String.html#method.from_utf8_lossy) if they're not valid unicode. That typically means you'll raise an error later when they're not recognized.

## Why?

For a particular application I was looking for a small parser that's pedantically correct. There are other compact argument parsing libraries, but I couldn't find one that handled `OsString`s and implemented all the fiddly details of the argument syntax faithfully.

This library may also be useful if a lot of control is desired, like when the exact argument order matters or not all options are known ahead of time. It could be considered more of a lexer than a parser.

## Why not?

This library may not be worth using if:

- You don't care about non-unicode arguments
- You don't care about exact compliance and correctness
- You don't care about code size
- You do care about great error messages
- You hate boilerplate

## See also

- [Collected benchmarks of argument parsing crates](https://github.com/rosetta-rs/argparse-rosetta-rs).
- libc's `getopt`
- Plan 9's *arg(3)*macros

# lexopt 0.1.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/lexopt/0.1.0

# Lexopt

Lexopt is an argument parser for Rust. It tries to have the simplest possible design that's still correct. It's so simple that it's a bit tedious to use.

Lexopt is:

- Small: one file, no dependencies, no macros. Easy to audit or vendor.
- Correct: standard conventions are supported and ambiguity is avoided. Tested and fuzzed.
- Pedantic: arguments are returned as `OsString`
- Imperative: options are returned as they are found, nothing is declared ahead of time.
- Annoyingly minimalist: only the barest necessities are provided.
- Unhelpful: there is no help generation and error messages often lack context.

## Example

```
```
Let's walk through this:

- We start parsing with `Parser::from_env()`.
- We call `parser.next()`in a loop to get all the arguments until they run out.
- We match on arguments. `Short`and`Long`indicate an option.
- To get the value that belongs to an option (like `10`in`-n 10`) we call`parser.value()`.- This returns a standard `OsString`
- For convenience, `use lexopt::prelude::*`adds a`.parse()`method, analogous to`str::parse`

- This returns a standard
- `Value`indicates a free-standing argument. In this case, a filename.- `if thing.is_none()`is a useful pattern for positional arguments. If we already found- `thing`we pass it on to another case.
- It also contains an `OsString`.- The standard `.into_string()`method can decode it into a plain`String`.

- The standard

- If we don't know what to do with an argument we use `return Err(arg.unexpected())`to turn it into an error message.
- Strings can be promoted to errors for custom error messages.

This covers almost all the functionality in the library. Lexopt does very little for you.

For a larger example with useful patterns, see [ examples/cargo.rs](https://docs.rs/examples/cargo.rs).

## Command line syntax

The following conventions are supported:

- Short options (`-q`)
- Long options (`--verbose`)
- `--`to mark the end of options
- `=`to separate long options from values (- `--option=value`)
- Spaces to separate options from values (`--option value`,`-f value`)
- Unseparated short options (`-fvalue`)
- Combined short options (`-abc`to mean`-a -b -c`)

These are not supported:

- `-f=value`for short options
- Options with optional arguments (like GNU sed's `-i`, which can be used standalone or as`-iSUFFIX`)
- Single-dash long options (like find's `-name`)
- Abbreviated long options (GNU's getopt lets you write `--num`instead of`--number`if it can be expanded unambiguously)

## Unicode

This library supports unicode while tolerating non-unicode arguments.

Short options may be unicode, but only a single codepoint. (If you need whole grapheme clusters you can use a long option. If you need normalization you're on your own, but it can be done.)

Options can be combined with non-unicode arguments. That is, `--option=���` will not cause an error or mangle the value. This is surprisingly tricky to support: see [ os_str_bytes](https://crates.io/crates/os_str_bytes).

Options themselves are patched as by [ String::from_utf8_lossy](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/string/struct.String.html#method.from_utf8_lossy) if they're not valid unicode. That typically means you'll raise an error later when they're not recognized.

## Why?

For a particular application I was looking for a small parser that's pedantically correct. There are other compact argument parsing libraries, but I couldn't find one that handled `OsString`s and implemented all the fiddly details of the argument syntax faithfully.

This library may also be useful if a lot of control is desired, like when the exact argument order matters or not all options are known ahead of time. It could be considered more of a lexer than a parser.

## Why not?

This library may not be worth using if:

- You don't care about non-unicode arguments
- You don't care about exact compliance and correctness
- You don't care about code size
- You do care about great error messages
- You hate boilerplate

## See also

- `clap`- `structopt`
- `argh`- `gumdrop`
- `pico-args`
- `ap`
- libc's `getopt`

# Parser in lexopt - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/lexopt/latest/lexopt/struct.Parser.html

`pub struct Parser { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A parser for command line arguments.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Get the next option or positional argument.

A return value of `Ok(None)` means the command line has been exhausted.

Options that are not valid unicode are transformed with replacement
characters as by [ String::from_utf8_lossy](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html#method.from_utf8_lossy).

[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

[ Error::UnexpectedValue](https://docs.rs/enum.Error.html#variant.UnexpectedValue) is returned if the last option had a
value that hasn’t been consumed, as in

`--option=value` or `-o=value`.It’s possible to continue parsing after an error (but this is rarely useful).

```
17fn main() -> Result<(), lexopt::Error> {
18    use lexopt::prelude::*;
19
20    let mut parser = lexopt::Parser::from_env();
21    parser.set_short_equals(false);
22    let mut free = Vec::new();
23    while let Some(arg) = parser.next()? {
24        match arg {
25            Short('n') | Long("number") => {
26                let num: u16 = parser.value()?.parse()?;
27                println!("Got number {}", num);
28            }
29            Long("shout") => {
30                println!("Got --shout");
31            }
32            Value(val) => {
33                free.push(val);
34                free.extend(parser.raw_args()?);
35            }
36            _ => return Err(arg.unexpected()),
37        }
38    }
39    println!("Got free args {:?}", free);
40    Ok(())
41}
```

9fn main() -> Result<(), lexopt::Error> {
10    use lexopt::prelude::*;
11
12    let mut settings = GlobalSettings {
13        toolchain: "stable".to_owned(),
14        color: Color::Auto,
15        offline: false,
16        quiet: false,
17        verbose: false,
18    };
19
20    let mut parser = lexopt::Parser::from_env();
21    while let Some(arg) = parser.next()? {
22        match arg {
23            Long("color") => {
24                settings.color = parser.value()?.parse()?;
25            }
26            Long("offline") => {
27                settings.offline = true;
28            }
29            Long("quiet") => {
30                settings.quiet = true;
31                settings.verbose = false;
32            }
33            Long("verbose") => {
34                settings.verbose = true;
35                settings.quiet = false;
36            }
37            Long("help") => {
38                println!("{}", HELP);
39                std::process::exit(0);
40            }
41            Value(value) => {
42                let value = value.string()?;
43                match value.as_str() {
44                    value if value.starts_with('+') => {
45                        settings.toolchain = value[1..].to_owned();
46                    }
47                    "install" => {
48                        return install(settings, parser);
49                    }
50                    value => {
51                        return Err(format!("unknown subcommand '{}'", value).into());
52                    }
53                }
54            }
55            _ => return Err(arg.unexpected()),
56        }
57    }
58
59    println!("{}", HELP);
60    Ok(())
61}

63#[derive(Debug)]
64struct GlobalSettings {
65    toolchain: String,
66    color: Color,
67    offline: bool,
68    quiet: bool,
69    verbose: bool,
70}
71
72fn install(settings: GlobalSettings, mut parser: lexopt::Parser) -> Result<(), lexopt::Error> {
73    use lexopt::prelude::*;
74
75    let mut package: Option<String> = None;
76    let mut root: Option<PathBuf> = None;
77    let mut jobs: u16 = get_no_of_cpus();
78
79    while let Some(arg) = parser.next()? {
80        match arg {
81            Value(value) if package.is_none() => {
82                package = Some(value.string()?);
83            }
84            Long("root") => {
85                root = Some(parser.value()?.into());
86            }
87            Short('j') | Long("jobs") => {
88                jobs = parser.value()?.parse()?;
89            }
90            Long("help") => {
91                println!("cargo install [OPTIONS] CRATE");
92                std::process::exit(0);
93            }
94            _ => return Err(arg.unexpected()),
95        }
96    }
97
98    println!("Settings: {:#?}", settings);
99    println!(
100        "Installing {} into {:?} with {} jobs",
101        package.ok_or("missing CRATE argument")?,
102        root,
103        jobs
104    );
105
106    Ok(())
107}

Get a value for an option.

This function should normally be called right after seeing an option
that expects a value, with positional arguments being collected
using [ next()](https://docs.rs/struct.Parser.html#method.next).

A value is collected even if it looks like an option
(i.e., starts with `-`).

[§](https://docs.rs#errors-1)Errors

An [ Error::MissingValue](https://docs.rs/enum.Error.html#variant.MissingValue) is returned if the end of the command
line is reached.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/lexopt/lib.rs.html#459-475)#### pub fn [values](https://docs.rs#method.values)(&mut self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[ValuesIter](https://docs.rs/struct.ValuesIter.html)<'_>, [Error](https://docs.rs/enum.Error.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/lexopt/lib.rs.html#459-475)

#### pub fn [values](https://docs.rs#method.values)(&mut self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[ValuesIter](https://docs.rs/struct.ValuesIter.html)<'_>, [Error](https://docs.rs/enum.Error.html)>

Gather multiple values for an option.

This is used for options that take multiple arguments, such as a
`--command` flag that’s invoked as `app --command echo 'Hello world'`.

It will gather arguments until another option is found, or `--` is found, or
the end of the command line is reached. This differs from `.value()`, which
takes a value even if it looks like an option.

On success the resulting iterator will yield at least one value.

An equals sign (`=`) will limit this to a single value. That means `-a=b c` and
`--opt=b c` will only yield `"b"` while `-a b c`, `-ab c` and `--opt b c` will
yield `"b"`, `"c"`.

(If [ short_equals](https://docs.rs/struct.Parser.html#method.set_short_equals) is disabled then

`-a=b c` will yield
`"=b"`, `"c"`.)[§](https://docs.rs#errors-2)Errors

If not at least one value is found then [ Error::MissingValue](https://docs.rs/enum.Error.html#variant.MissingValue) is returned.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
let arguments: Vec<OsString> = parser.values()?.collect();
let at_most_three_files: Vec<PathBuf> = parser.values()?.take(3).map(Into::into).collect();
for value in parser.values()? {
    // ...
}
```
Take raw arguments from the original command line.

This returns an iterator of [ OsString](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/ffi/os_str/struct.OsString.html)s. Any arguments that are not
consumed are kept, so you can continue parsing after you’re done with
the iterator.

To inspect an argument without consuming it, use [ RawArgs::peek](https://docs.rs/struct.RawArgs.html#method.peek) or

[.](https://docs.rs/struct.RawArgs.html#method.as_slice)

`RawArgs::as_slice`[§](https://docs.rs#errors-3)Errors

Returns an [ Error::UnexpectedValue](https://docs.rs/enum.Error.html#variant.UnexpectedValue) if the last option had a left-over
argument, as in

`--option=value`, `-ovalue`, or if it was midway through
an option chain, as in `-abc`. The iterator only yields whole arguments.
To avoid this, use [.](https://docs.rs/struct.Parser.html#method.try_raw_args)

`try_raw_args()`After this error the method is guaranteed to succeed, as it consumes the rest of the argument.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-1)Example

As soon as a free-standing argument is found, consume the other arguments as-is, and build them into a command.

```
Value(prog) => {
    let args: Vec<_> = parser.raw_args()?.collect();
    let command = std::process::Command::new(prog).args(args);
}

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/lexopt/lib.rs.html#608-614)#### pub fn [try_raw_args](https://docs.rs#method.try_raw_args)(&mut self) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[RawArgs](https://docs.rs/struct.RawArgs.html)<'_>>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/lexopt/lib.rs.html#608-614)

#### pub fn [try_raw_args](https://docs.rs#method.try_raw_args)(&mut self) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[RawArgs](https://docs.rs/struct.RawArgs.html)<'_>>

Take raw arguments from the original command line, *if* the current argument
has finished processing.

Unlike [ raw_args()](https://docs.rs/struct.Parser.html#method.raw_args) this does not consume any value
in case of a left-over argument. This makes it safe to call at any time.

It returns `None` exactly when [ optional_value()](https://docs.rs/struct.Parser.html#method.optional_value)
would return

`Some`.Note: If no arguments are left then it returns an empty iterator (not `None`).

[§](https://docs.rs#example-2)Example

Process arguments of the form `-123` as numbers. For a complete runnable version of
this example, see
[ examples/nonstandard.rs](https://github.com/blyxxyz/lexopt/blob/e3754e6f24506afb42394602fc257b1ad9258d84/examples/nonstandard.rs).

```
fn parse_dashnum(parser: &mut lexopt::Parser) -> Option<u64> {
    let mut raw = parser.try_raw_args()?;
    let arg = raw.peek()?.to_str()?;
    let num = arg.strip_prefix('-')?.parse::<u64>().ok()?;
    raw.next(); // Consume the argument we just parsed
    Some(num)
}
loop {
    if let Some(num) = parse_dashnum(&mut parser) {
        println!("Got number {}", num);
    } else if let Some(arg) = parser.next()? {
        match arg {
            // ...
        }
    } else {
        break;
    }
}
```
The name of the command, as in the zeroth argument of the process.

This is intended for use in messages. If the name is not valid unicode
it will be sanitized with replacement characters as by
[ String::from_utf8_lossy](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html#method.from_utf8_lossy).

To get the current executable, use [ std::env::current_exe](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/env/fn.current_exe.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#example-3)Example

```
let mut parser = lexopt::Parser::from_env();
let bin_name = parser.bin_name().unwrap_or("myapp");
println!("{}: Some message", bin_name);
```

#### pub fn [optional_value](https://docs.rs#method.optional_value)(&mut self) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[OsString](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/ffi/os_str/struct.OsString.html)>

Get a value only if it’s concatenated to an option, as in `-ovalue` or
`--option=value` or `-o=value`, but not `-o value` or `--option value`.

Create a parser from the environment using [ std::env::args_os](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/env/fn.args_os.html).

This is the usual way to create a `Parser`.

```
17fn main() -> Result<(), lexopt::Error> {
18    use lexopt::prelude::*;
19
20    let mut parser = lexopt::Parser::from_env();
21    parser.set_short_equals(false);
22    let mut free = Vec::new();
23    while let Some(arg) = parser.next()? {
24        match arg {
25            Short('n') | Long("number") => {
26                let num: u16 = parser.value()?.parse()?;
27                println!("Got number {}", num);
28            }
29            Long("shout") => {
30                println!("Got --shout");
31            }
32            Value(val) => {
33                free.push(val);
34                free.extend(parser.raw_args()?);
35            }
36            _ => return Err(arg.unexpected()),
37        }
38    }
39    println!("Got free args {:?}", free);
40    Ok(())
41}
```

7fn parse_args() -> Result<Args, lexopt::Error> {

49fn parse_args() -> Result<AppArgs, lexopt::Error> {
50    use lexopt::prelude::*;
51
52    let mut number = None;
53    let mut opt_number = None;
54    let mut width = 10;
55    let mut input = None;
56
57    let mut parser = lexopt::Parser::from_env();
58    while let Some(arg) = parser.next()? {
59        match arg {
60            Short('h') | Long("help") => {
61                print!("{}", HELP);
62                std::process::exit(0);
63            }
64            Long("number") => number = Some(parser.value()?.parse()?),
65            Long("opt-number") => opt_number = Some(parser.value()?.parse()?),
66            Long("width") => width = parser.value()?.parse_with(parse_width)?,
67            Value(path) if input.is_none() => input = Some(path.into()),
68            _ => return Err(arg.unexpected()),
69        }
70    }
71    Ok(AppArgs {
72        number: number.ok_or("missing required option --number")?,
73        opt_number,
74        width,
75        input: input.ok_or("missing required argument INPUT")?,
76    })
77}

9fn main() -> Result<(), lexopt::Error> {
10    use lexopt::prelude::*;
11
12    let mut settings = GlobalSettings {
13        toolchain: "stable".to_owned(),
14        color: Color::Auto,
15        offline: false,
16        quiet: false,
17        verbose: false,
18    };
19
20    let mut parser = lexopt::Parser::from_env();
21    while let Some(arg) = parser.next()? {
22        match arg {
23            Long("color") => {
24                settings.color = parser.value()?.parse()?;
25            }
26            Long("offline") => {
27                settings.offline = true;
28            }
29            Long("quiet") => {
30                settings.quiet = true;
31                settings.verbose = false;
32            }
33            Long("verbose") => {
34                settings.verbose = true;
35                settings.quiet = false;
36            }
37            Long("help") => {
38                println!("{}", HELP);
39                std::process::exit(0);
40            }
41            Value(value) => {
42                let value = value.string()?;
43                match value.as_str() {
44                    value if value.starts_with('+') => {
45                        settings.toolchain = value[1..].to_owned();
46                    }
47                    "install" => {
48                        return install(settings, parser);
49                    }
50                    value => {
51                        return Err(format!("unknown subcommand '{}'", value).into());
52                    }
53                }
54            }
55            _ => return Err(arg.unexpected()),
56        }
57    }
58
59    println!("{}", HELP);
60    Ok(())
61}
```
Create a parser from an iterator. This is useful for testing among other things.

The first item from the iterator **must** be the binary name, as from [ std::env::args_os](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/env/fn.args_os.html).

The iterator is consumed immediately.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-4)Example

`let mut parser = lexopt::Parser::from_iter(&["myapp", "-n", "10", "./foo.bar"]);`[Source](https://docs.rs/src/lexopt/lib.rs.html#828-830)#### pub fn [set_short_equals](https://docs.rs#method.set_short_equals)(&mut self, on: [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html))

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/lexopt/lib.rs.html#828-830)

#### pub fn [set_short_equals](https://docs.rs#method.set_short_equals)(&mut self, on: [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html))

Configure whether to parse an equals sign (`=`) for short options.

If this is **true** (the default), `-o=foobar` will be interpreted as
the option `-o` with the value `foobar`.

If this is **false**, `-o=foobar` will be interpreted as
the option `-o` with the value `=foobar`.

Note that even if this is `true` the equals sign is optional. That is,
`-ofoobar` and `-o foobar` are always interpreted as `-o` with the value
`foobar` regardless of this setting.

Most other argument parsers treat the equals sign as part of the value,
but the syntax is notably accepted by [ clap](https://docs.rs/clap/latest/clap/)
and by Python’s

[.](https://docs.python.org/3/library/argparse.html)

`argparse`You may want to disable this setting if it’s common for an option’s value
to start with an equals sign. The Unix `cut` command for example is sometimes
used with `-d=`, where `"="` is the value belonging to the `-d` option. By default
the empty string `""` is parsed instead.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-5)Example

You can configure this right after creating the parser:

```
let mut parser = lexopt::Parser::from_env();
parser.set_short_equals(false);
```
You could also do it temporarily, for an individual option:

```
Short('d') | Long("delimiter") => {
    parser.set_short_equals(false);
    delimiter = Some(parser.value()?.string()?);
    parser.set_short_equals(true);
}
```
```
17fn main() -> Result<(), lexopt::Error> {
18    use lexopt::prelude::*;
19
20    let mut parser = lexopt::Parser::from_env();
21    parser.set_short_equals(false);
22    let mut free = Vec::new();
23    while let Some(arg) = parser.next()? {
24        match arg {
25            Short('n') | Long("number") => {
26                let num: u16 = parser.value()?.parse()?;
27                println!("Got number {}", num);
28            }
29            Long("shout") => {
30                println!("Got --shout");
31            }
32            Value(val) => {
33                free.push(val);
34                free.extend(parser.raw_args()?);
35            }
36            _ => return Err(arg.unexpected()),
37        }
38    }
39    println!("Got free args {:?}", free);
40    Ok(())
41}

# lexopt 0.3.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/lexopt/latest/source/DESIGN.md

```
Some rambling thoughts that don't deserve a place in the README.
The API consists of a handful of clean simple powerful methods with no arguments and no configurability, plus some more junk to make them convenient to use.
Language features are to be preferred over library features as much as possible. That way the library can stay smaller and code that uses the library is hopefully easier to understand in detail for people who aren't familiar with the library.
I don't really like the `ValueExt` extension trait, but I can't think of a nicer way to parse values. In my ideal workflow you would call `.into_string()?.parse()?` to parse a value, all built-in methods. But I don't think it's possible to have an error type that can be transformed from both methods' error types, `into_string` returns `OsString` and there are annoying rules around overlapping trait implementations. The error messages would also suffer.
(Update: as of 0.3.0, `ValueExt` has a `string` method as an alternative to `into_string` with a cleaner return type. In theory this opens the way to removing `From<OsString>`, but I don't think `lexopt::Error` should be catch-all. There's `anyhow` for that.)
Keeping the core API clean and generic means this could perhaps be used as the basis of a more complete parser.
POSIX has a notion of subarguments, combining multiple values in a single option-argument by separating them with commas or spaces. This is easy enough to hand-roll for valid unicode (`.into_string()?.split(...)`) but we could provide a function that does it on `OsString`s. I can't think of a case where values may not be valid unicode but definitely don't contain commas or spaces, though.
Sometimes Rust is a bother.
`Arg::Long` contains a borrowed string instead of an owned string because you can't match owned strings against string literals. That means `Arg` needs a lifetime, the iterator protocol cannot be used (it would also be a bad fit for other reasons), and some abstractions are hard or impossible to build. On the plus side, error messages can be slightly better.
(Deref patterns would fix this, and if/when they're released I'll probably do a breaking release with a huge MSRV bump. I consider them a prerequisite for 1.0.)
Arguments on Windows sometimes have to be transcoded three times: from UTF-16 to WTF-8 by `args_os`, then back to UTF-16 to parse them, then to WTF-8 again to be used. This ensures we see the original invalid code unit if there's a problem, but it's a bit sad. (Luckily it only happens very rarely.)
There's not always enough information for a good error message. A plain `OsString` doesn't remember what the parser knows, like what the last option was.
`ValueExt::parse` exists to include the original string in an error message and to wrap all errors inside a uniform type. It's unclear if it earns its upkeep.
I see three ways to store `Parser`'s internal iterator:
1. 2.3.
lexopt originally used option 2 but switched to option 3.
**Option 1** (generic field) is the most general and powerful but it's cumbersome and bloated. Benefits:
- --
Drawbacks:
- --
**Option 2** (trait object) doesn't have the drawbacks of option 1, but it reduces everything to a lowest common denominator:
- --
**Option 3** (known type) means collecting the iterator into a `Vec` when the parser is constructed and then turning that into an iterator.
- --
There are also drawbacks:
- --  -
lexopt could not originally be configured. As of writing it has a single setting, [`set_short_equals`](https://docs.rs/lexopt/latest/lexopt/struct.Parser.html#method.set_short_equals). This setting is pretty niche but there's no way to implement it in user code.
There's also a request to [make `.value()` ignore arguments that look like options](https://github.com/blyxxyz/lexopt/issues/14) but this can be emulated by calling `.values()` in a wacky way.
Both settings are potentially context-sensitive. An option might need to take negative numbers as values, or arbitrary filenames. That means you might want to switch the option on/off just for the duration of parsing a single option. This is one reason that the setting was implemented as a `&mut self` method on `Parser`. However, you have to remember to revert the configuration once you're done.
Other possible APIs are:
- --
I don't expect any more settings beyond `set_short_equals`. If the need does arise they can hopefully use the same signature.
These are all defensible design choices, they're just a bad fit for some of the programs I want to write. All of them make some other kind of program easier to write.
- ----
These make the library simpler and smaller, which is the whole point.
clap is very large, both in API surface and in code size.
It also [used](https://github.com/blyxxyz/lexopt/blob/d00be2711096c088cf198650d8853b2420516be3/DESIGN.md#clapstructopt) to suffer from bad defaults for OS strings and options that take multiple values. These problems are solved in current versions. (It still doesn't nudge people toward OS strings the way lexopt does but that's very reasonable.)
Despite the size and complexity it's my personal first choice for complicated interfaces.
The current MSRV is 1.31, the first release of the 2018 edition.
The blocker for moving it even earlier was non-lexical lifetimes, there's some code that won't compile without it.
The `Value(arg) if foo.is_none() =>` pattern doesn't actually work until 1.39 ([`bind_by_move_pattern_guards`](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/63118)), so not all of the examples compile on the MSRV. (And one of them uses `str::strip_prefix`, which requires at least 1.45.)
All these versions are very old. The MSRV will be raised dramatically once there is any reason to do so. Right now there isn't.
```

# lexopt 0.3.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/lexopt/latest/source/README.md

```
[![Crates.io](https://img.shields.io/crates/v/lexopt.svg)](https://crates.io/crates/lexopt)
[![API reference](https://docs.rs/lexopt/badge.svg)](https://docs.rs/lexopt/)
[![MSRV](https://img.shields.io/badge/MSRV-1.31-blue)](https://blog.rust-lang.org/2018/12/06/Rust-1.31-and-rust-2018.html)

Lexopt is an argument parser for Rust. It tries to have the simplest possible design that's still correct. It's so simple that it's a bit tedious to use.
Lexopt is:
- -----
```rust
struct Args {
}
fn parse_args() -> Result<Args, lexopt::Error> {
}
fn main() -> Result<(), lexopt::Error> {
}
```
Let's walk through this:
- ---  -    -  --  -  -    ---
This covers most of the functionality in the library. Lexopt does very little for you.
For a larger example with useful patterns, see [`examples/cargo.rs`](examples/cargo.rs).
The following conventions are supported:
- ---  ------
These are not supported out of the box:
- -
[`Parser::raw_args()`](https://docs.rs/lexopt/latest/lexopt/struct.Parser.html#method.raw_args) and [`Parser::try_raw_args()`](https://docs.rs/lexopt/latest/lexopt/struct.Parser.html#method.try_raw_args) provide an escape hatch for consuming the original command line. This can be used for custom syntax, like treating `-123` as a number instead of a string of options. See [`examples/nonstandard.rs`](examples/nonstandard.rs) for an example of this.
This library supports unicode while tolerating non-unicode arguments.
Short options may be unicode, but only a single codepoint (a `char`).
Options can be combined with non-unicode arguments. That is, `--option=���` will not cause an error or mangle the value.
Options themselves are patched as by [`String::from_utf8_lossy`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/string/struct.String.html#method.from_utf8_lossy) if they're not valid unicode. That typically means you'll raise an error later when they're not recognized.
For a particular application I was looking for a small parser that's pedantically correct. There are other compact argument parsing libraries, but I couldn't find one that handled `OsString`s and implemented all the fiddly details of the argument syntax faithfully.
This library may also be useful if a lot of control is desired, like when the exact argument order matters or not all options are known ahead of time. It could be considered more of a lexer than a parser.
This library may not be worth using if:
- ----

# lexopt - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/lexopt/latest/target-redirect/lexopt/index.html

## Expand description

A pathologically simple command line argument parser.

Most argument parsers are declarative: you tell them what to parse, and they do it.

This one provides you with a stream of options and values and lets you figure out the rest.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
struct Args {
    thing: String,
    number: u32,
    shout: bool,
}
fn parse_args() -> Result<Args, lexopt::Error> {
    use lexopt::prelude::*;
    let mut thing = None;
    let mut number = 1;
    let mut shout = false;
    let mut parser = lexopt::Parser::from_env();
    while let Some(arg) = parser.next()? {
        match arg {
            Short('n') | Long("number") => {
                number = parser.value()?.parse()?;
            }
            Long("shout") => {
                shout = true;
            }
            Value(val) if thing.is_none() => {
                thing = Some(val.string()?);
            }
            Long("help") => {
                println!("Usage: hello [-n|--number=NUM] [--shout] THING");
                std::process::exit(0);
            }
            _ => return Err(arg.unexpected()),
        }
    }
    Ok(Args {
        thing: thing.ok_or("missing argument THING")?,
        number,
        shout,
    })
}
fn main() -> Result<(), lexopt::Error> {
    let args = parse_args()?;
    let mut message = format!("Hello {}", args.thing);
    if args.shout {
        message = message.to_uppercase();
    }
    for _ in 0..args.number {
        println!("{}", message);
    }
    Ok(())
}
```
Let’s walk through this:

- We start parsing with `Parser::from_env`
- We call `parser.next()`
- We match on arguments. `Short``Long`
- To get the value that belongs to an option (like `10`in`-n 10`) we call`parser.value()`- This returns a standard `OsString`
- For convenience, `use lexopt::prelude::*``.parse()``str::parse`
- Calling `parser.value()`is how we tell`Parser`that`-n`takes a value at all.

- This returns a standard
- `Value`indicates a free-standing argument.- `if thing.is_none()`is a useful pattern for positional arguments. If we already found- `thing`we pass it on to another case.
- It also contains an `OsString`.- The `.string()``String`.

- The

- If we don’t know what to do with an argument we use `return Err(arg.unexpected())`
- Strings can be promoted to errors for custom error messages.

# lexopt/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)//! A pathologically simple command line argument parser.
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//!
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//! Most argument parsers are declarative: you tell them what to parse,
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//! and they do it.
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//!
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//! This one provides you with a stream of options and values and lets you
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//! figure out the rest.
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//!
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//! ## Example
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//! ```no_run
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//! struct Args {
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//!     thing: String,
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//!     number: u32,
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//!     shout: bool,
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//! }
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//!
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//! fn parse_args() -> Result<Args, lexopt::Error> {
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//!     use lexopt::prelude::*;
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//!
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//!     let mut thing = None;
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//!     let mut number = 1;
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//!     let mut shout = false;
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//!     let mut parser = lexopt::Parser::from_env();
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//!     while let Some(arg) = parser.next()? {
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//!         match arg {
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//!             Short('n') | Long("number") => {
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//!                 number = parser.value()?.parse()?;
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//!             }
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//!             Long("shout") => {
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//!                 shout = true;
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//!             }
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//!             Value(val) if thing.is_none() => {
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//!                 thing = Some(val.string()?);
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//!             }
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//!             Long("help") => {
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//!                 println!("Usage: hello [-n|--number=NUM] [--shout] THING");
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//!                 std::process::exit(0);
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//!             }
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//!             _ => return Err(arg.unexpected()),
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//!         }
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//!     }
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//!
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//!     Ok(Args {
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//!         thing: thing.ok_or("missing argument THING")?,
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//!         number,
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//!         shout,
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//!     })
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//! }
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//!
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//! fn main() -> Result<(), lexopt::Error> {
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//!     let args = parse_args()?;
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//!     let mut message = format!("Hello {}", args.thing);
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//!     if args.shout {
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//!         message = message.to_uppercase();
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//!     }
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//!     for _ in 0..args.number {
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//!         println!("{}", message);
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//!     }
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//!     Ok(())
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//! }
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//! ```
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//! Let's walk through this:
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//! - We start parsing with [`Parser::from_env`].
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//! - We call [`parser.next()`][Parser::next] in a loop to get all the arguments until they run out.
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//! - We match on arguments. [`Short`][Arg::Short] and [`Long`][Arg::Long] indicate an option.
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//! - To get the value that belongs to an option (like `10` in `-n 10`) we call [`parser.value()`][Parser::value].
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//!   - This returns a standard [`OsString`].
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//!   - For convenience, [`use lexopt::prelude::*`][prelude] adds a [`.parse()`][ValueExt::parse] method, analogous to [`str::parse`].
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//!   - Calling `parser.value()` is how we tell `Parser` that `-n` takes a value at all.
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//! - `Value` indicates a free-standing argument.
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//!   - `if thing.is_none()` is a useful pattern for positional arguments. If we already found `thing` we pass it on to another case.
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//!   - It also contains an `OsString`.
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//!     - The [`.string()`][ValueExt::string] method decodes it into a plain `String`.
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//! - If we don't know what to do with an argument we use [`return Err(arg.unexpected())`][Arg::unexpected] to turn it into an error message.
[75](https://docs.rs#75)//! - Strings can be promoted to errors for custom error messages.
[76](https://docs.rs#76)

[103](https://docs.rs#103)    state: State,
[104](https://docs.rs#104)    /// The last option we emitted.
[105](https://docs.rs#105)    last_option: LastOption,
